articles.title: Ghost Rovers: I Called 12 Machines NASA Left Behind. One Picked Up.
articles.description: A 1969 Mission Control console for kids. Built in one day for NASA Space Apps 2026.   TL;DR: For NASA...
articles.body_html:
A 1969 Mission Control console for kids. Built in one day for NASA Space Apps 2026.

TL;DR: For NASA Space Apps 2026 I built Ghost Rovers, a free web app where kids sit at a 1969 Mission Control console and call the 12 machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars. Five Moon machines answer NO SIGNAL, the Apollo 11 Laser Mirror answers, and Mars stays quiet. I directed it in one day, with Claude planning and checking and Google Antigravity building, and every fact traces back to NASA's own records.

The first commit went in at 10:47 a.m. PST on Saturday: a 15-minute test to see whether my phone could spin a 3D Moon without choking. At 7:32 p.m. I clicked Submit for Judging. In between, the project grew a second planet, a study kit for teachers, a 27-second demo video with Apollo radio beeps, and one correction I'm glad I asked for.

NASA Space Apps is NASA's global hackathon, run over one weekend. This year one of the challenges was called Abandoned but not Forgotten: tell the story of the hardware NASA has left on the Moon and Mars, for school-age space fans. The challenge text even suggested "an interactive map of the Moon with clickable ghost rovers." I didn't have to look any further.

Why this one? I love helping people, teaching people, and learning. Kids hear about rockets launching. They almost never hear about what stayed behind. The facts all exist in NASA's catalog, but they read like a spec sheet: catalog IDs, coordinates, mass budgets. Nobody tells a 9-year-old that a car has been parked on the Moon since before their grandparents had cell phones. lol

earlgreyhot1701D / ghost-rovers

Ghost Rovers

12 machines are still on the Moon and Mars. Only 1 still answers.

A 1969 Mission Control console where kids ages 8 to 12 radio the hardware NASA left behind, on the Moon and on Mars.

Play it live · Watch the 27-second demo · Slides (PDF) · Go to Mars · Study notebook · Fact check · SI disclosure

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Abandoned but not Forgotten · Team Clew Labs (La Shara Cordero)

The problem

Kids hear about rockets launching. They almost never hear about what stayed behind. The facts are all in NASA's catalog, but they read like a spec sheet: COSPAR IDs, coordinates, mass budgets. Nobody tells a 9-year-old that a car has been parked on the Moon since before their grandparents had cell phones.

What Ghost Rovers does

You sit at a Mission Control console. Six machines are out there. You…

View on GitHub

Pick one. Press CALL GHOST.

You sit at a Mission Control console. Six machines are out there on the Moon. You pick one and press CALL GHOST. Radio static. Then:

On the Moon Today
Surveyor 3 Quiet since 1967
Apollo 11 Laser Mirror Still answers
Eagle's launch pad Resting since 1969
Apollo 12 moonquake station Switched off 1977
Apollo 15 Rover Parked since 1971
Apollo 17 Rover Parked since 1972

Five reply NO SIGNAL with the year they went quiet. One answers. Scientists on Earth still bounce lasers off the Apollo 11 mirror, so the console draws a beam from Earth to the Moon and back, and the round trip takes 2.5 seconds, the real number.

Press M and the console flips to Mars: Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight. None of them answer. Yet.

Each machine has a file: its original mission, a short story in its own voice, three questions kids ask ("Could I drive it?" "What's it made of?"), its real NASA photo, and a live counter of how long it has been sitting there, down to the second. READ TO ME reads the file out loud. Call all six on a world and you earn a Junior Flight Controller badge you can save.

The console had to look like 1969

I spent the first real block of the day on design, before any build. Claude mocked up three directions: Museum After Dark, Field Notebook, and Mission Control 1969. I picked Mission Control, then sent the first version back because it didn't look enough like 1969. The second pass got the details: amber clocks, a red label-maker tape, a curved wall screen, console sounds generated in code instead of recorded.

Then I wrote one rule into the agent's instructions before it built anything: the design is like-for-like. Build what was approved. If you have an improvement, list it separately and don't build it until I say yes. I've had agents "clean up" a design into something generic before, and I wasn't going to spend the afternoon arguing with a button radius.

Every fact had to survive NSSDCA

NSSDCA, NASA's Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, keeps a record for every mission. Every date, landing site, and status in Ghost Rovers was checked line by line against those records, and both fact-check logs are public in the repo.

The check caught real overclaims. A draft called the Apollo 15 rover "the first car on the Moon." The Soviet Union's robot rover, Lunokhod 1, got there in 1970, a year earlier. The line now reads "the first car astronauts drove on the Moon." That kind of fix is small on screen and it's the whole difference between a fun app and a fun app a teacher can trust.

The same rule applied to the Mars clock. "Light time Earth to Mars: 3 to 22 minutes" comes from NASA's Mars fact sheet: the closest and farthest Earth distances, divided by the speed of light.

Two agents, one notebook, one rule

I don't write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I check and decide. Here's who did what on Saturday:

Who What they did
Me The idea, the kid audience, the 1969 look, every design call, every yes or no
Claude (Opus 5.5) The plan, design mockups, fact checks against NSSDCA, an independent check after every block, the docs, the demo video and slides
Google Antigravity Built the site in small blocks: propose a plan, wait for my approval, then build
Google's Gemini Notebook A public study notebook from the same NASA sources: a quiz, flashcards, and a mind map for each world, plus a podcast with AI voices

The rhythm worked. Antigravity proposed, I approved, it built, Claude checked the result in a real browser at three screen sizes and ran an accessibility scan, and only then did the next block start. Claude's checks caught things that read fine in code and looked wrong on screen: the Earth sitting inside the Moon during the laser animation, a badge title clipped off the edge, an answer box covering the story text.

The friction was mostly plumbing. Antigravity's built-in browser couldn't take screenshots on my machine, so it switched to a headless script. Old editor tabs kept trying to save stale copies of files over new ones. Once I learned to close the tab and pick Don't Save, that stopped.

Space Apps calls AI tools "Super Intelligence," or SI, and asks you to label anything SI made. So every code file has a one-line SI header, every SI-assisted image and video carries a visible label, and the repo has a full disclosure log of what each tool did.

The rule was in the wrong file

Around 4 p.m., Claude ran a code review and pointed out that main.js was 1,104 lines and main.css was 2,775. I loathe god files. My build rules say one file, one job.

Then we found out why. The rule lived in the file Claude reads. It never made it into the file Antigravity reads on every block. So Antigravity did the reasonable thing and kept adding each new feature to the files that already existed, block after block, and Claude's checks were looking at whether things worked, not at how big the files were getting.

We split the CSS into nine files, all under 500 lines, and proved the split changed nothing: the joined files match the original line for line, and before and after screenshots at three screen sizes came out identical. The two big JavaScript files stay as they are until after the hackathon. Each one is a single giant function, and splitting that the night before a deadline is how you break the thing judges are about to open. They're listed in the agent instructions now as known exceptions, with a 500-line rule for everything else.

"Yet" needed a meaning

By 7 p.m. I was writing the project description, and something in my own pitch bugged me. Mars: none of them answer. Yet. What do we do with "yet"?

That question turned up a mistake. Claude's draft of the description said no machine on Mars answers. That isn't true. Curiosity has been driving around Gale Crater since 2012, and Perseverance has been working in Jezero Crater since 2021. In October, Perseverance broke Opportunity's off-world driving record. The six machines in Ghost Rovers are quiet. Mars is not.

My first instinct was to make Curiosity and Perseverance callable, like the Laser Mirror. Claude advised against it, and I agreed: the challenge is about discarded equipment, and those two are working missions with teams driving them every day. Calling them ghosts would stretch the theme and break "only 1 still answers" everywhere at once.

So they became the answer to "yet" instead. Finish the Mars check, and the badge panel adds one more row:

Antigravity usage was running low by then, so Claude built that row itself, as a new file with one job so the big files stayed untouched, and Antigravity committed it. The Mars clock already said "People on Mars: none yet," so "yet" ended up meaning what it should have meant all along: nobody has visited these machines. The next voice from those landing sites could be a kid watching today.

Thirty seconds, with Apollo radio beeps

The demo had to be 30 seconds or less, so Claude built a 27-second film in the app's own look: the console powering on, the Laser Mirror call, the switch to Mars, and a closing card with the classroom kit.

The sound is my favorite part. Claude logged every sound the app made while a script played it, the clicks, the static, the laser ping, the NO SIGNAL buzz, and rebuilt them at the exact moments they happened. I asked for more Mission Control, so it added Quindar tones, the short beeps you hear on Apollo-era Mission Control radio audio. The narration is a synthetic voice, labeled on screen and in the file. The video is on YouTube.

The form fought back

The last bug of the day wasn't in the app. Claude filled in 15 NASA data links on the submission form by typing them, and a check afterward found the typing had dropped letters: display.ction instead of display.action, in several URLs. It reset all 15 and checked them again. Later, a second editor tab I'd left open almost saved an older, emptier version over the finished one. Reload, don't save. Lesson learned twice in one evening.

What it can't do

  • No human voice yet. A real Mission Control voice, ghost names, and Spanish are the v2 list.
  • The podcast covers the Moon only.
  • Two JavaScript files are still far over my own 500-line rule.
  • Phone and tablet checks ran in browser emulation, not on every real device. I tested on my own Android phone.
  • Twelve machines is a start. NASA has left a lot more out there.

Try it

Play Ghost Rovers, or go straight to Mars. Keys 1 to 6 pick a machine, C calls it, M flips worlds. No login, no tracking, no data collected.

For teachers: the study notebook has a quiz, flashcards, and a mind map for each world, and it's public.

The numbers, from the repo on submission day:
Machines 12 (6 Moon, 6 Mars)
Answering 1 (plus 2 working rovers linked on Mars)
Accessibility scan (axe-core, WCAG 2.1 AA) 0 violations on both worlds
First commit to submit 10:47 a.m. to 7:32 p.m.
Commits by submission 21

Space Apps sent me a participant certificate that says Galactic Problem Solver. That one's going on the wall.

Did a machine answer when you called it? I'd love to hear which one you tried first.

Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I don't write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide. I build the Clew Suite, a set of civic tech tools for making complex systems easier to inspect.

Built with AI assistance in November 2026. NASA facts link to NASA's own records, and the fact-check logs are in the repo. These tools move fast, so check the source before you quote me.

AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

articles.title: Avengers: Doomsday is 5 weeks away, so I built hexagon README badges. What are you building?
articles.description: Marvel fans of DEV, show me your Doomsday-hype side projects. Mine is a tiny Vercel service that makes glowing, Avengers-themed hexagon badges.
articles.body_html:
Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18, 2026. That's about five weeks from now, and I figured the best use of the wait was to build something Marvel-flavored instead of just rewatching trailers.

So I made hex-badges: hexagon README badges with 10 Avengers-inspired color themes, a glow effect, and live GitHub stats. Yes, one of the themes is a green-and-silver Latveria badge. Doom deserves a README badge.

Before the technical stuff, I have a question for the Marvel fans on DEV: what are you building (or have you built) with the Doomsday hype? A themed portfolio, a countdown widget, a Discord bot, a game, a dumb little CLI? Drop it in the comments. I would love to see them. More on that at the end.

  • Live demo and badge builder: https://hex-badges.vercel.app
  • Source: https://github.com/amananandrai/hex-badges

What you get

Two badge styles, 10 themes, and every badge is a plain SVG served from a URL:

![stars](https://hex-badges.vercel.app/github/stars/facebook/react?theme=stark-forge)
![license](https://hex-badges.vercel.app/github/license/facebook/react?theme=asgard&style=wide)
  • Single hexagon: label over value, with a glow and a themed pattern.
  • Elongated: a two-part badge with a pointed hexagon outline, closer to a classic badge.

GitHub metrics: stars, forks, watchers, open issues, open PRs, latest release, latest tag, last commit, license, contributors, language and repo size. There is also a custom endpoint, /api/badge?label=build&message=passing, for anything else.

How it works

The whole thing is three small pieces, and none of them needs a dependency.

1. An SVG renderer. A badge is just a string. For the single hexagon, the six corner points come from a bit of trigonometry:

const ring = (rad) => [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((k) => {
  const a = ((-90 + 60 * k) * Math.PI) / 180;
  return `${cx + rad * Math.cos(a)},${cy + rad * Math.sin(a)}`;
}).join(' ');
// <polygon points="${ring(r)}" .../>

The tricky part of any badge generator is text width. Real services measure font metrics. I estimate it from character count, which is good enough for a short label:

const textWidth = (s, size) => Math.ceil(String(s).length * size * 0.62);

For long values the hexagon is capped at a maximum size and the font shrinks to fit.

2. Serverless functions on Vercel. Each endpoint reads query params and returns SVG with caching headers:

res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'image/svg+xml; charset=utf-8');
res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=300, s-maxage=300');
res.status(200).send(svg);

A vercel.json rewrite turns /github/stars/owner/repo into a function call, so the URLs stay short.

3. GitHub data. Each metric is a small function that calls the GitHub REST API and returns a message. Counts are shortened (12,437 becomes 12.4k), and errors become badges too, such as "not found" or "rate limited", instead of a broken image.

Making the themes feel right

Each theme is a handful of values: two gradient pairs, text colors, an outline color and a glow color. Gradients give the badges a metallic look, so "silver" and "gold" actually read as metal.

The glow is the fun part. SVG has no simple glow property, so it is a filter that floods the shape's outline with a color, blurs it, and merges it under the original:

<filter id="glow" x="-40%" y="-40%" width="180%" height="180%">
  <feFlood flood-color="#37ff86" result="f"/>
  <feComposite in="f" in2="SourceAlpha" operator="in" result="c"/>
  <feGaussianBlur in="c" stdDeviation="4" result="b"/>
  <feMerge>
    <feMergeNode in="b"/><feMergeNode in="b"/>
    <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
  </feMerge>
</filter>

On top of that, each single hexagon gets a pattern clipped to its shape with a clipPath: arc-reactor rings, armor plates and rivets, lightning, a woven lattice, stars and stripes, cracks, a targeting reticle, a spider web, a sling-ring mandala, and cosmic dust with six colored stones. I kept patterns away from the text area so values stay readable.

One deliberate choice: I used generic motifs and my own theme names, not logos or official symbols. These badges are inspired by the colors, and they are not affiliated with Marvel or Disney.

Lessons learned

  • Escape everything. Labels come from the URL and go into an SVG, so any user-supplied text is escaped before it is inserted. Otherwise a crafted URL can inject markup.
  • Validate the repo param. My first regex accepted ../evil as an owner/repo, which would have sent a path-traversal-style request to the GitHub API. A test caught it. Now . and .. segments are rejected.
  • Cache hard. Badges get requested constantly. CDN cache headers keep latency low and API usage small.
  • Plan for rate limits. GitHub allows only 60 unauthenticated requests per hour per IP, and serverless platforms share IPs. A read-only token with no scopes raises that to 5,000 per hour. Issue and PR counts use the search API, which has its own tighter limit, so caching matters even more there.
  • Glow needs a dark background. On GitHub's dark theme the glow looks great. On white it fades to a soft halo, which still looks fine but is more subtle.

Deploy your own

  1. Fork the repo and import it into Vercel. There is no build step.
  2. Create a fine-grained GitHub token with public repositories, read-only access and no permissions.
  3. Add it in Vercel as the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable and redeploy.

That's it. The landing page at / has a builder where you pick a theme and copy the Markdown.

What's next

More metrics (npm versions and downloads are next on my list), more themes, and a light-background glow variant. Theme requests are open, and that's where I need you.

Your turn: let's make this a Doomsday watercooler

Pick any of these and answer in the comments. One line is plenty.

  1. Show me your Marvel (or Doomsday) project. Link the repo, the site, or just describe it, however rough or silly. Hype projects count.
  2. Which theme is your favorite? Stark Forge, Latveria, Asgard, Wakanda, Star Shield, Gamma Smash, Red Room, Web Slinger, Mystic Arts or Infinity.
  3. Which theme should I add next? X-Men, Fantastic Four, Loki, Scarlet Witch, something from the DC side? Give me a color combo and a pattern idea and I'll try to build it.
  4. Are you Team Avengers or Team Doom? Defend your answer. Bonus points if you argue it using only README badges.
  5. Post your README. Add a badge to one of your repos and share a screenshot. I'll reply to as many as I can.

And if you are not a Marvel person, tell me about the side project you are most excited about right now. This is a watercooler post, so all fun projects are welcome.

Disclaimer: this is a fan project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Marvel or Disney. Theme names are my own, and the patterns are generic motifs, not official logos.

articles.title: One Tool Call Instead of Four Pages: Adding WebMCP to My Site
articles.description: AI agents that open debbie.codes in a browser can now use tools on the page to find my videos, posts, podcasts and courses, instead of reading whole pages and guessing.
articles.body_html:
This post is about how I added WebMCP to debbie.codes, how you can try it, and how it compares to the other ways agents read websites.

WebMCP lets a site offer tools in the browser, so an agent can ask the page a question and get a short, structured answer instead of reading whole pages and guessing.

I built it with Cursor cloud agents, coordinated by my Grok Bot site lead, and I reviewed and merged the changes. It already runs for real visitors in Chrome and Edge.

Prefer to watch? Here's the video, where I show the tools in the Chrome DevTools WebMCP panel.

What is WebMCP

WebMCP is a proposed web standard. A page registers tools with the browser. Each tool has a name, a description, a JSON Schema for its inputs and an execute function. An agent working in the browser can then find those tools and call them, instead of clicking around and reading the page. On my site that's document.modelContext.registerTool(). Older examples use navigator.modelContext, but the spec puts it on document now. Playwright's WebMCP docs still use navigator.modelContext. You can read more in the Chrome WebMCP docs.

A few things worth knowing:

  • It's being worked on in the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group. There's an explainer and a draft spec.
  • There are two ways to add tools: an imperative JavaScript API, which is what I used, and a declarative API using HTML forms.
  • WebMCP doesn't replace MCP. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open-source standard for connecting AI apps to external systems. Chrome describes MCP as the backend and WebMCP as the frontend. An MCP server works anywhere, while WebMCP tools only exist while the page is open in a tab. Chrome explains the difference in WebMCP vs MCP.
  • Right now it's available through an origin trial, in Chrome from version 149 and in Edge. An origin trial gives a site access to a new or experimental feature for a limited time, using a trial key from the browser. For local work Chrome has a flag, chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing.
  • Chrome's docs say it's mainly meant for when a person is there in the browser with the agent, not for scripts that drive a browser with no one watching. Agents also have to visit the page to discover its tools.

Why I wanted it

My content is spread across videos, blog posts, podcasts and courses, each with their own tag pages. When an agent browses my site for someone, it needs a reliable way to answer "what has Debbie done on this topic?".

Videos are the richest part, and the best answer is often "minute 29 of this talk". No page on my site shows that.

What an agent gets from it

When I tried my videos page with ChatGPT, it listed what the tools gave it compared to reading the page. I checked each point against my code:

  • Precise filters. It called list-videos, one of my site's tools, with the tag mcp instead of guessing the topic from titles.
  • More than what's on screen. The tool reported 27 matching videos, while the page only showed a few.
  • Structured results. Each video comes back with its title, date, link, tags, conference and host as separate fields.
  • Fewer clicks. One call replaced clicking through filters and pages.
  • Easier discovery. Each tool's description tells the agent what it's for and which inputs to use.
  • Deeper search. search-content also searches chapter titles and links straight to that minute of the video. For the full chapter list of one video, get-video pages through them.

So my site decides how agents find and understand my content, including details like chapters that are hard to find on the page itself.

What I built

The site builds one JSON index of all my content when it's generated, and five tools read from it:

  • list-videos lists my videos, newest first, filtered by tag, conference or host.
  • topic-brief sums up how much I've published on one topic across videos, posts, podcasts and courses, with counts, dates and a few highlights.
  • search-content searches across everything.
  • get-video returns one video by YouTube id, including its chapters, and pages through them if there are many.
  • get-current-page tells the agent what the page it's on is about and what's related.

A few details I care about:

  • All five tools are read only. Nothing on the site changes, and each tool says so with readOnlyHint.
  • Every answer stays under 2,000 characters. List, search and get-video results page with hasMore and nextOffset. If a page is still too big, the tool shortens it and sets trimmed, so the agent can ask for the next page.
  • Errors are sentences. If you ask for "playwrite", you get "No content matched topic 'playwrite'. Closest tags: playwright." instead of an exception.
  • Video results link to the right minute. I copied the YouTube chapter markers into the index, so a search for "healer agent" returns a link straight to the "The Healer Agent" chapter of my talk. Chapters only come from YouTube's own markers or timestamps in the description, and a video needs at least two. Nothing is made up.
  • No extra load for normal visitors. If the browser doesn't support WebMCP, the site checks once and stops. The tool code and the content index never load.

Here is the check that skips WebMCP for everyone else:

export default defineNuxtPlugin(() => {
  const mc = document.modelContext
  if (!mc || typeof mc.registerTool !== 'function')
    return

  const api = { registerTool: mc.registerTool.bind(mc) }
  import('~/utils/webmcp/register')
    .then(({ registerWebMCPTools }) => registerWebMCPTools(api))
    .catch(() => {})
})

And one of the tool definitions:

topicBrief: {
  name: 'topic-brief',
  description: 'Summarizes how much Debbie has published on one topic across videos, posts, podcasts, and courses. Use when the task needs counts, a date range, and a few highlights.',
  inputSchema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: { topic: { type: 'string', maxLength: 80 } },
    required: ['topic'],
    additionalProperties: false,
  },
  annotations: { readOnlyHint: true },
},

That object only describes the tool. When the site registers it, it adds the execute function, which is what runs when an agent calls the tool:

for (const [tool, execute] of tools)
  await mc.registerTool({ ...tool, execute }, { signal })

The signal comes from an AbortController, so the tools can be removed again later. If you're starting from scratch, Chrome's Imperative API guide has complete registerTool examples.

The same build step also writes the site's llms.txt files. I go through those in Get your site agent-ready, along with the markdown copies of each post.

Origin trials let normal Chrome and Edge users get the API on my site without turning on a flag. The site adds two origin trial meta tags, one for Chrome and one for Edge. The origin trial keys in those tags only work on debbie.codes, so the tags are only added to the production build. A small check:origin-trial script runs in CI, builds the production site and fails unless both tags are in the HTML.

Try it yourself

In Chrome or Edge on debbie.codes

On debbie.codes you don't need any flag. The origin trial switches the API on. I checked this on Chrome 157 stable with no flags.

  1. Use Chrome 150 or newer, or a current version of Edge. Chrome 149 has the API, but its DevTools WebMCP pane still needed flags.
  2. Open debbie.codes and view the source. You should see two <meta http-equiv="origin-trial"> tags.
  3. Open the DevTools console and run await document.modelContext.getTools(). You should see all five tools. To call one, run: 
const tools = await document.modelContext.getTools()
const brief = tools.find(t => t.name === 'topic-brief')
await document.modelContext.executeTool(brief, { topic: 'mcp' })

When I ran topic-brief with mcp it took 19 ms. Try the same on example.com and document.modelContext doesn't exist, because there's no origin trial there.

  1. You can do the same without code in the DevTools WebMCP pane.
    1. If you don't see the Application tab, press Ctrl+Shift+P (Command+Shift+P on a Mac) and choose Show Application.
    2. Select WebMCP in the Application sidebar.
    3. The Available tools list shows all five tools with their descriptions. Click topic-brief, enter mcp next to topic and click Run tool.
    4. The call shows up under Tool activity with its input and output.
    5. If Available tools is empty, WebMCP isn't on for that page, for example on localhost without the testing flag. The DevTools WebMCP panel docs have more.

On localhost or a preview site

The origin trial keys only work on debbie.codes, so turn on chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing, restart Chrome and use the DevTools panel. Edge has the same flag at about://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing.

From code with Playwright

My tests use Playwright's WebMCP API, added in Playwright 1.64. Launch Chromium with --enable-features=WebMCP. You need that even on the live site. The origin trial turns on document.modelContext, but page.webmcp refuses to run without the flag. Then:

await page.goto('https://debbie.codes/')
const tools = await page.webmcp.tools()
const brief = await page.webmcp.callTool('topic-brief', { topic: 'mcp' })

From an MCP client with chrome-devtools-mcp

Another option is chrome-devtools-mcp, an MCP server that lets a coding agent control and inspect a live Chrome browser. It has experimental list_webmcp_tools and execute_webmcp_tool tools behind the --categoryExperimentalWebmcp flag.

Without WebMCP

You can also start with debbie.codes/llms.txt. I walk through those files in Get your site agent-ready.

Try it with an AI agent

ChatGPT calls WebMCP tools site tools. OpenAI's help page says they work in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser, and they're available when your account has access and the website provides site tools.

This is how I tried it:

  1. In ChatGPT, open the mode selector, choose Work, and ask it to open https://debbie.codes/videos.
  2. Then ask: "Discover the tools exposed by this website and use list-videos to find videos tagged mcp."

The first half of that prompt is tool discovery, where the agent lists the tools the page exposes. The second half calls one of those tools, list-videos.

Two things to know:

  • Having the page open in Work's browser doesn't always mean WebMCP tool discovery is on, so it may just click around the page instead.
  • Site tools are only available to accounts that have access.

To call the tools from code or a coding agent instead, see the Playwright and chrome-devtools-mcp parts of Try it yourself above. Puppeteer also has an experimental WebMCP API on page.webmcp, with its own WebMCP guide.

Google says Gemini in Chrome will support WebMCP soon, so more agents should be able to use these tools.

The numbers

The numbers below were measured on 13 November 2026. Token counts use OpenAI's o200k_base tokenizer, so other models will count a little differently.

Asking "what has Debbie published on MCP?"

Before WebMCP, an agent answering this opened four tag pages and still had to count everything by hand. Now one tool call answers it in about 562 tokens.

How Requests What the agent reads
Read the four MCP tag pages as HTML 4 256,713 bytes, about 99,013 tokens
Read the visible text of those four pages 4 about 2,764 tokens
Call topic-brief 1 1,900 characters, about 562 tokens

And the tool answer already has the counts, the first and latest dates and a link to the listing page. This run returned 7 of 46 highlights to fit the size limit. With the pages, the agent still has to count and sort, and it gets no chapter times.

The first tool call takes about 10 ms, because the index loads as soon as the tools register, and visitors without WebMCP never load it.

I haven't measured how long a full task takes with a real agent, or how many tokens a screenshot based agent would use, so I'm not claiming numbers for those.

How it compares to other ways agents read a site

Method How it works Trade offs
Reading the HTML Load each listing page and parse it 4 page loads, no counts, no chapter times, and it breaks when the layout changes
Screenshots and clicking Look at the screen and click filters The problem WebMCP is meant to solve. I didn't measure it
A remote MCP server The agent connects to a server Works without the site open, but it's another service to host, secure and keep in sync, and the user has to set it up
llms.txt Read one text file Great for discovery, and I ship one. A static file can't be queried and has no chapters, even when the full catalog lists everything. See Get your site agent-ready and llmstxt.org
WebMCP tools One call to a typed tool in the open tab One call returns a full answer, with checked inputs, chapter links and read only tools. Only works while the page is open, in a browser that supports it

I did both. llms.txt is the static first step, and I wrote about that in Get your site agent-ready. The WebMCP tools are for agents already on the page. Both come from the same build time index, so they can't drift apart.

What I'd tell you before adding WebMCP to your site

  • Use a static index if your site is static. A JSON file is fast, cacheable and the same everywhere.
  • Build small tools with one job each. Give each one a description that says when to use it. Chrome's best practices say the same.
  • Cap the answer size, and say what you left out. Keep answers small so they don't fill the model's context. Always return the real total and a way to get the next page, so an agent never mistakes a short list for the full answer. Make errors full sentences an agent can act on.
  • Make tools read only where you can, and say so.
  • Never make up data. If a video has no chapters, it has no chapters.
  • Don't slow the site down for everyone else. Feature detect first and load nothing if the browser doesn't support it.

Open debbie.codes in ChatGPT's browser and ask it to discover the tools on the page and use them to find something about my work, like my MCP videos. If you have a site of your own, try adding a tool or two. It's a small step, and I'd love to hear what you build.

articles.title: I built a workspace that reads my body, then asked it to leave me alone
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.           What I Built   Most...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.

What I Built

Most "smart" developer tools add things: another panel, another badge, another notification. I wanted the opposite. ZenDev is a developer workspace that removes friction when I am calm and adds exactly one thing when I am not: a breath.

It measures pulse, heart-rate variability, breathing and, when the SDK reports them, facial expressions and skin conductance through the Presage SmartSpectra SDK. It learns what calm looks like for me, then expresses everything else as a single relative number: a 0–100% load index. The interface cools and opens up when that number is low. When it climbs, lines loosen, the palette warms, and the bio-timeline records it.

The part I care about most is the guardrail. A destructive command typed into the sandbox shell — rm -rf, git reset --hard, DROP TABLE — does not run while load is in strain. Instead a breathing ring appears, and the proceed button stays disabled until I have taken one full breath. The same rule is available inside VS Code through a companion extension.

Why relative, not absolute

The SDK gives absolute values — beats per minute, RMSSD in milliseconds, breaths per minute — and it is very easy to build a dashboard that tells people they are stressed. I do not think that is honest. Resting heart rate differs by tens of beats between healthy people, and HRV varies with age, fitness and the time of day.

So ZenDev spends its first ten seconds building a baseline from confident readings only. Every value after that is a difference from that baseline: each metric's delta is normalised and clamped to 0–1, then weighted into the load index. A pulse of 85 is not "high". A pulse of 85 when your calm median is 61 is a signal.

That choice changes the whole app. There is no red state by default, no score to optimise, and no population comparison. There is only "you, right now, compared to you ten minutes ago".

Demo

Watch the demo

The demo shows the app receiving live camera input, the signal rail displaying pulse, breathing rate and HRV with confidence, the load index rising above the guardrail threshold, the breathing gate, and the VS Code status bar. It also labels the one boundary clearly: the shell inside ZenDev is a simulated sandbox, while the VS Code command runs in a real terminal.

Code

Repository: github.com/Emanuelmsjv/zendev

Requirements: Node 22.12+ and a Presage API key.

git clone https://github.com/Emanuelmsjv/zendev
cd zendev
npm install
cp .env.example .env      # add SMARTSPECTRA_API_KEY
npm start

There is no ZenDev account or login. Camera input needs a Presage API key; after accepting consent, the clearly labelled simulator is available without one for exploring the interface. npm run app runs the Vite dev server with hot reload. The VS Code extension lives in vscode-extension/ and installs as a .vsix; the README has the one-line commands. Camera and phone input require the Electron build.

How It Responds to Human Signals

ZenDev uses live SmartSpectra signals end to end:

  • cardio.pulseRate for pulse
  • cardio.hrv.rmssd for HRV
  • breathing.rate for breathing rate
  • face.expression for facial tension
  • eda.trace for skin-conductance slope

The last two are used when the extended face/EDA models are available. If they are not, the app retries with pulse, HRV and breathing and says which signals it is using. It never invents a missing value.

The pipeline is:

phone or laptop camera
   → Presage SmartSpectra SDK (breathing + cardio + face + EDA)
   → per-field cache with 8 s freshness, EMA smoothing with rate limits
   → ten-second personal baseline and weighted load index
   → theme, meter, signal rail, bio-timeline, terminal guardrail, VS Code status bar

Two implementation details mattered more than I expected.

Partial payloads. The SDK emits different metrics on different frames. Dropping the last packet when hrv is missing made the meter jump. Each metric now carries its own timestamp and confidence, and a value is reused for up to eight seconds before it is shown as missing. A stale number is labelled, never invented.

Two time constants. Load rises faster than it falls: a 1.2 s attack and a 5 s release. A single bad frame no longer repaints the app, and the guardrail does not flap.

The response is visible in real time. The palette, line height and letter spacing interpolate with load. The signal rail exposes the live SDK output instead of hiding it behind a single score. The bio-timeline marks commits, runs, phase changes and guardrail events. In VS Code, the extension reads the current load from a guard-state file and shows one status-bar item; if the file is older than fifteen seconds, the item disappears so a dead app never leaves a stale number behind.

The guardrail is deliberately easy to bypass. It is a speed bump for the version of me that types git reset --hard at 96% load, not a security control.

Prize Categories

I am entering both:

  • Most Creative or Delightful Use. The workspace does not display a stress dashboard and ask me to interpret it. It changes how the editor feels, then turns a destructive command into a breathing pause. The unexpected part is that the reward for a high reading is not more data — it is a moment of stillness.
  • Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. Developers already lose work to rushed destructive commands. ZenDev addresses that moment with a personal baseline, visible live signals, explicit consent, local-only processing, and a deletion path that removes stored data. It is designed for one person at one desk, not for surveillance or medical decision-making.

Consent and Data Handling

Camera access is opt-in. On first run, ZenDev shows a consent screen that explains what it reads, what leaves the machine, and what it keeps. The camera and phone options remain disabled until the consent checkbox is ticked and an API key is present; the simulator is available after consent without a key. The app shows a visible LIVE, PHONE or SIMULATED indicator while a session is running.

What leaves the machine. ZenDev does not upload camera frames or measured metrics. The SDK contacts Presage only to authenticate the API key, validate the subscription, and fetch on-device models when needed. Metric computation runs on-device. SDK telemetry is explicitly disabled with enableTelemetry: false, so no session summaries or device-readiness reports are sent. There is no optional AI service.

What is stored. Consent state, settings (including the API key), and a rolling session trace of the latest 3,600 samples plus commit markers live in the app's local storage profile. The desktop app also writes a small guard-state file to ~/.zendev/guard.json and to its Electron userData directory so the VS Code extension can read the live load. That file contains only load, phase, confidence, threshold and timestamps. Exports are written only when the user chooses a path.

Retention and deletion. There is no server-side retention. Local data stays until it is deleted. Delete data stops the session, clears ZenDev's local storage, and removes both guard-state files. Deleting data does not revoke the API key with Presage; that is done in the Presage account.

This is a relative-arousal experience, not a diagnosis or treatment tool. A high number means "different from your baseline", not unwell. No reading is used for medical decision-making, and nothing is monitored without the user starting the session.

Built for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge. If you try it, tell me whether the breathing gate feels like a pause or like a punishment — that is the part I am least sure about.

articles.title: ChatGPT Stopped Recommending This App Overnight. The Culprit Was a Domain Move (and One Regex)
articles.description: For weeks, ChatGPT was quietly acting as an iOS app's best salesperson, sending roughly a third of...
articles.body_html:
For weeks, ChatGPT was quietly acting as an iOS app's best salesperson, sending roughly a third of all its downloads. Then, almost overnight, it went silent.

No bad review. No App Store penalty. No new version. Nothing in the app had changed.

The website had moved to a new address. It was a routine, by-the-book migration, the kind that's usually forgotten by lunchtime. Within days, the app's biggest traffic source had dropped to close to zero, and total downloads were cut in half.

Here's how a "harmless" domain move wiped out a ChatGPT traffic source, the one-line regex bug that quietly made it worse, and the checklist that would have prevented all of it.

The "textbook" migration

The app is a small iPhone utility with a marketing site: a homepage, feature pages, comparison pages and about a dozen how-to guides. The site was originally served from a Cloudflare Workers subdomain (something.workers.dev).

In early October it was rebuilt with Astro and moved to a Cloudflare Pages subdomain (something.pages.dev). As part of the rebuild:

  • canonical tags, og:url, JSON-LD, the sitemap and robots.txt all switched to the new host
  • URLs changed shape: /guides/foo.html became /guides/foo, and /guides/ became /guides
  • the old Workers host became a small redirect Worker that sends visitors to the new host

On paper, it was flawless. In practice, it was about to go badly wrong.

The day the referrals stopped

App Store Connect reports first-time downloads by source. One source is App Referrer, meaning another app sent the user to the App Store, and ChatGPT appears there by name.

Period Share of downloads from App Referrer (mostly ChatGPT) Daily downloads
Several weeks before the move roughly a third baseline
A couple of weeks after the move close to zero roughly half of baseline

App Store search dipped only modestly, so the main loss was ChatGPT. The referrals stopped within days of the canonical change. (All figures here are rounded on purpose.)

This is a correlation, not a controlled experiment. Still, no other change lined up: the listing, keywords and app version stayed the same through that window.

Why AI assistants punish a domain move harder than Google does

ChatGPT's web answers rely heavily on Bing's index. When a page that recommended the app was indexed under the old host, ChatGPT could find it, cite it and link to the App Store.

After the move:

  1. The old URLs told Bing "the real page is now elsewhere" (new canonicals and redirects).
  2. The new host was brand new to Bing: no history and no inbound links.
  3. Bing didn't hand the old pages' standing to the new host quickly. The old pages lost value, and the new ones had none yet.

Google handled it a bit better and indexed the new homepage within a few weeks. Bing's URL Inspection showed something more worrying:

Blocked – URL cannot appear on Bing.
"The inspected URL is known to Bing but has some issues which are preventing us from serving it."

The Live URL test for the same page passed: "URL can be indexed by Bing", "No SEO/GEO issues found". So it wasn't a technical block. It was a quality or trust decision about a new, unlinked site, and the Bing dashboard said as much: "Your site lacks inbound links from high-quality domains."

The one-line bug hiding in plain sight

The redirect Worker on the old host looked roughly like this:

const TARGET = 'https://new-host.example';

// Some pages must still be served in place (older app builds load them in a web view).
const PROXIED_PAGES = new Set(['/privacy', '/terms']);

// "Assets" are proxied so the proxied pages can load CSS and images.
const isAsset = (pathname) =>
  pathname.startsWith('/_astro/') || /\.[a-z0-9]+$/i.test(pathname);

export default {
  async fetch(request) {
    const { pathname, search } = new URL(request.url);
    if (PROXIED_PAGES.has(pathname) || isAsset(pathname)) {
      return fetch(TARGET + pathname + search);   // served as 200
    }
    return Response.redirect(TARGET + pathname + search, 301);
  },
};

Spot it? It's easy to miss. The "is it an asset?" regex matches any file extension, including .html. Every old /guides/foo.html URL, which were exactly the URLs search engines had indexed, was proxied with a 200 instead of redirected with a 301.

So the old host kept serving full copies of every page, while those copies' canonical tags pointed at the new host. To a crawler, that looks like two sites with the same content, one of them disowning itself. That's a good way to make a search engine distrust both.

The fix is small: exclude HTML from the asset rule, and map old URL shapes straight to the final URL in one hop.

const isAsset = (pathname) =>
  pathname.startsWith('/_astro/') ||
  (/\.[a-z0-9]+$/i.test(pathname) && !/\.html?$/i.test(pathname));

// /index.html → /, /guides/ → /guides, /guides/foo.html → /guides/foo
const canonicalPath = (pathname) => {
  let path = pathname.replace(/\/index\.html?$/i, '/').replace(/\.html?$/i, '');
  if (path.length > 1 && path.endsWith('/')) path = path.slice(0, -1);
  return path || '/';
};

// ...
return Response.redirect(TARGET + canonicalPath(pathname) + search, 301);

A quick way to test every legacy URL, using the old sitemap from git history:

while read p; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$p -> %{http_code} %{redirect_url}\n" "https://old-host.example$p"
done < old-paths.txt

Every line should show 301 pointing at the matching new URL. Following the redirect (curl -L) should end on a 200.

Two more traps waiting in Search Console

  • Google Search Console showed "Couldn't fetch" for a sitemap that worked. The sitemap returned 200 with valid XML, even when fetched with a Googlebot user agent. The status stayed stuck with no "Last read" date for over a week. It's a known display quirk on new properties: the file is fine, Google just hasn't fetched it yet. Resubmitting with a query string (sitemap-0.xml?v=2) creates a new entry, and robots.txt should list the sitemap anyway.
  • "Request indexing" hit "Quota exceeded" on the very first click. On new properties this happens often. Don't fight it: the sitemap and internal links from an already-indexed page do the same job without a quota.

The checklist that would have saved the traffic

  1. Don't move unless you have to. If the old address is indexed and cited, its history is an asset.
  2. If you move, move once, ideally to a domain you own. Shared hosts like *.pages.dev or *.workers.dev start with little trust, and every later move resets it.
  3. Redirect every old URL with a single 301 to its exact new equivalent. Test the real legacy URLs (from the old sitemap in git), not just the homepage.
  4. Never serve full copies of pages from the old host, even by accident through an asset rule.
  5. Set up Bing Webmaster Tools and Google Search Console before the move, not after. Bing has a site-move tool, and you'll want the before-and-after data.
  6. Use IndexNow to tell Bing about changed URLs immediately.
  7. Plan for inbound links. A new host with no backlinks may be crawled but not shown. Directory listings, launch sites and a few relevant articles help.

Where it stands now

The redirect fix is live, every legacy URL now returns a clean 301, a Bing review has been requested, and the backlink work has started. Recovery isn't guaranteed or quick. Search engines rebuild trust over weeks, not days. A follow-up will share what actually brought the traffic back.

The app in this story is Clean Kit, an iPhone photo and storage cleaner that runs entirely on-device. It's on the App Store.
