articles.body_html:
Far away in the galaxy, there was a beautiful planet called necoz. 🌌

One day, the King of necoz announced something very exciting:

📢 Attention, everyone! Today we are hosting the biggest Cat Party in the entire galaxy! All cats are invited!

Cats from different galaxies started arriving. Some came by UFO, some came by spaceship, and one cat even arrived on a flying pizza! 🍕

🛸 Scene 1: 30 Cats and a Confused King

The party finally started.

The King looked around and shouted:

WHAT?! There are 30 cats here! Who is going to count all of them?

Suddenly, a little cat wearing sunglasses said:

Bro, just use Python!

The King opened his laptop and wrote:

cats = 30

print(cats)

Output:

30

The King: "WOW! Python counted them without even asking for their names!"

And that's how the King discovered Variables.

A variable is like a container that stores information.

In this example:

  • cats is the variable name.
  • 30 is the value.
  • = is the assignment operator.

🍕 Scene 2: 10 More Hungry Cats!

Suddenly, a UFO landed near the party.

10 more cats came out.

Their leader shouted:

WE WANT FOOD! WE ARE STARVING!

The King replied:

Bro, this is a party, not a free restaurant!

He updated his Python code:

cats = 30

cats = 40

print(cats)

Output:

40

The King: "WAIT! We had 30 cats, and now we have 40!"

That's the magic of variables. We can change the value stored in a variable.

🎂 Scene 3: The Great Cake Disaster

The King ordered 5 cakes for the party.

But one cat grabbed a cake and shouted:

THIS CAKE IS MINE!

Another cat replied:
NO! I SAW IT FIRST!

Meanwhile, a third cat(@hanzla ) was already escaping with the entire cake box. 😂

The King decided to store the information in separate variables.

cats = 40
cakes = 5

print(cats)
print(cakes)

Output:

40
5

Now Python knows that there are 40 cats and 5 cakes.

Each variable stores its own value.

😹 Scene 4: Different Types of Data

The King wanted to record more information about the party.

So he wrote:

planet = "necoz"
cats = 40
party_started = True
cake_price = 250.50

His assistant cat asked:

Why do these values look different?

The King explained:

Variable Value Data Type
planet "necoz" String
cats 40 Integer
party_started True Boolean
cake_price 250.50 Float

Let's understand them:

  • String: Stores text or words.
  • Integer: Stores whole numbers.
  • Boolean: Stores True or False.
  • Float: Stores decimal numbers.

The cat replied:

OMG! So I can also become a variable?

The King: "Yes, but please stop eating the cake!" 😂

💻 Scene 5: The Final Python Experiment

The King decided to display all the party information together.

planet = "necoz"
cats = 40
cakes = 5
party_started = True

print("Welcome to", planet)
print("Total Cats:", cats)
print("Total Cakes:", cakes)
print("Party Started:", party_started)

Output:

Welcome to necoz
Total Cats: 40
Total Cakes: 5
Party Started: True

The King shouted:

FINALLY! I AM A PYTHON DEVELOPER!

But suddenly, a cat @effessdev interrupted:
Developer later, bro. First, order 40 more cakes!

And that's how the biggest cat party in the galaxy continued all night. 🐱🎉

articles.title: Code Is Cheap Now. Judgment Isn't: The Review Bottleneck and the Vanishing Apprenticeship
articles.description: Writing code has become the cheapest part of software development. Understanding it hasn't.  Over the...
articles.body_html:
Writing code has become the cheapest part of software development. Understanding it hasn't.

Over the past year, AI assistants have changed the economics of producing code. A working endpoint, a migration script, or a set of unit tests can appear in seconds.

But software doesn't ship when code is written. It ships when someone is confident enough to put it in front of real users.

That gap between generated and trusted is where a lot of engineering teams are quietly struggling right now. And it raises a question that goes beyond tooling:

If AI absorbs the work that used to teach engineers judgment, where will the next generation of reviewers come from?

Let's look at the review bottleneck, the apprenticeship problem behind it, and what developers and teams can do about both.

1. Faster Generation Doesn't Mean Faster Delivery

Imagine a developer who opens six pull requests before lunch. Each one is clean, well-formatted, and passes CI.

Now imagine the people who have to review them.

A reviewer doesn't just read the diff. They have to understand the intent, reconstruct the context, and think about what the diff doesn't show:

The index that should exist but doesn't.

The race condition that only appears under concurrent writes.

The authorization check that is present, but applied to the wrong object.

The behavior change in a downstream service nobody mentioned.

Reviewing is slower than generating, and AI hasn't changed that nearly as much.

So when output volume goes up and review capacity stays flat, teams usually end up in one of three places:

Queues grow, and "fast" code sits waiting for days.

Reviews get shallower, and risk moves into production unnoticed.

Senior engineers become full-time reviewers and quietly burn out.

None of these show up as a productivity problem on a dashboard that counts pull requests opened.

2. Measure Outcomes, Not Output

If a team celebrates the number of tickets closed or lines generated, it will get more of both.

Whether the software is actually getting better is a different question, and it needs different signals:

Change failure rate: how often do deployments cause a problem?

Time to restore: how quickly can the team recover when something breaks?

Review time: how long does a change wait, and how deep is the review it receives?

Incident frequency: are we seeing fewer surprises, or more?

If an AI tool makes individuals feel faster while these numbers stay flat or worsen, the team isn't more productive. It may simply be borrowing against future incidents.

This doesn't mean the tools aren't useful. It means the claim "we're faster" should be tested against outcomes, not impressions.

3. The Apprenticeship Problem

Here is the part that worries me more than the review queue.

Many experienced engineers built their instincts the slow way. They wrote plenty of mediocre code early in their careers, debugged it at inconvenient hours, and gradually learned what wrong looks like.

They learned about performance by shipping a slow query. They learned about concurrency by causing a bug that only appeared on Fridays. They learned about failure modes by being the person on call when something fell over.

A lot of that learning happened through small, unglamorous tasks:

Fixing minor bugs.

Writing straightforward endpoints.

Adding tests to existing code.

Reading unfamiliar code and figuring out why it worked.

These tasks weren't just cheap labor. They were the training program.

If AI absorbs many of them, and companies respond by hiring fewer juniors, we risk a delayed problem. The people who would have become tomorrow's senior reviewers never get the experience that makes review possible.

That cost won't appear on this quarter's budget. It will show up years from now, when organizations discover they have plenty of generated code and not enough people who can judge it.

4. Judgment Is Built by Being Wrong

There's an uncomfortable idea here.

Engineering judgment is often presented as the durable advantage in the AI era. I believe that's largely true. But judgment isn't something you can read your way into.

It develops through a loop:

Make a decision.

See what happens.

Notice the gap between what you expected and what occurred.

Adjust your mental model.

Fluent, plausible AI output can weaken that loop. When code arrives looking polished and complete, a newer developer may not yet have the feel to recognize what's off. And if they never had to build it from scratch, they may have little to compare it against.

That doesn't mean juniors should avoid AI. It means the way they use it matters enormously.

5. Using AI to Learn Instead of Skip

There's a meaningful difference between using AI to understand something and using it to avoid understanding it.

A few habits that keep the learning loop intact:

Predict, then compare. Before asking for an implementation, write down how you think it should work and where it could fail. Then compare your prediction with the output. The gap between them is exactly what you need to study.

Keep a rejection log. Record AI suggestions you decided not to use, and why. "This query would have scanned the whole table" is a far better interview story than a polished repository with no history behind it.

Explain it back. If you can't explain why a generated solution works, in your own words and without looking at it, you don't own it yet.

Break it on purpose. Feed the code strange inputs, concurrent requests, and missing data. Learning what failure looks like is half of judgment.

Write the tests from the requirements. If the same tool writes both the function and the tests, the tests often just encode the function's assumptions. Derive test cases from what the code is supposed to do, then ask: what would have to be true for this test to fail?

None of this is slow. It's simply deliberate.

6. Portfolios That Show You've Operated Software

Earlier advice about building one substantial project still holds. But there's a refinement worth adding.

The most convincing projects aren't the ones that look the most polished. They're the ones where you can tell the author has actually operated the software.

That might mean:

A handful of real users, even a few friends or a small community.

A short incident write-up: what broke, how you found it, how you fixed it.

Notes on trade-offs you chose and what you'd do differently.

A changelog showing how the project evolved after real feedback.

A tutorial clone proves you can follow instructions. A small system with a postmortem proves you can debug, communicate, and learn from failure, which are exactly the skills teams struggle to find.

7. What Teams Can Do to Keep the Pipeline Alive

This can't only be an individual responsibility. Organizations that want experienced engineers in five years have to invest in producing them now.

Practical ways to do that:

Protect real learning work. Don't automate every small task away from juniors. Some of it is the curriculum.

Pair on purpose. Pairing and mentorship transfer the "why" behind decisions in a way documentation rarely does.

Make reviews teach. A review that explains the reasoning behind a comment is training. A review that just says "change this" isn't.

Give juniors real ownership. A small production service with real consequences, supported by a safety net, builds judgment faster than any exercise.

Plan for review capacity. If generation speeds up, review needs investment too: smaller changes, clearer descriptions, better automation, and protected time.

Preserve institutional knowledge. Document the systems, workarounds, and historical decisions that live only in a few people's heads, before those people are no longer around to explain them.

8. Can We Even Measure Judgment in Hiring?

There's a harder question underneath all of this.

If judgment is the valuable skill, how do hiring processes evaluate it?

Take-home projects can now be generated. Live coding interviews often measure performance under pressure more than long-term reasoning. Résumés list technologies, not decisions.

So the industry may be tempted to fall back on easy proxies: years of experience, brand-name employers, or credentials.

Better signals are possible, but they take more effort:

Ask candidates to walk through a past production issue and how it was reviewed afterward.

Give them a piece of flawed code (generated or not) and ask what concerns them.

Ask how they verify AI-assisted work, and what they've rejected.

Discuss a trade-off they made and what they'd change now.

Candidates can ask these questions too. A team's answer to "tell me about the last incident and how you learned from it" reveals a great deal about its culture, its ownership, and whether it's a place where you'd grow.

9. A Practical 30-Day Plan for Building Judgment

Judgment can't be rushed, but it can be practiced deliberately.

Week 1: Start a decision journal

For every meaningful task, note what you expected, what happened, and what surprised you. If you use AI, record your prediction before you see its answer.

Week 2: Review something you didn't write

Read an open-source pull request or a teammate's change. Write down what you would check, what you'd question, and what you can't judge yet. Those gaps are your study list.

Week 3: Break and fix something small

Take one of your own projects. Introduce a realistic failure (slow query, bad input, concurrent update), find it using logs and tests, then write a short postmortem.

Week 4: Share what you learned

Publish the postmortem, a rejection-log entry, or a short article. Teaching is one of the fastest ways to find out what you actually understand.

At the end of the month, you won't have mastered anything. But you'll have evidence of how you think, and that is what teams are increasingly trying to find.

Final Thoughts: Fast Code Still Needs Slow Learning

AI is making it easier than ever to produce code. That's genuinely useful, and ignoring it isn't a strategy.

But software engineering has never been only about producing code. It's about deciding what should exist, noticing what could go wrong, and taking responsibility for what reaches users.

Those abilities are built through experience: through being wrong, finding out why, and doing better next time.

If we let the tools replace the experiences that build judgment, we may end up with a profession that has plenty of output and fewer people qualified to trust it.

Developers can protect themselves by treating AI as a teacher rather than a shortcut. Teams can protect themselves by treating junior engineers as a long-term investment rather than a task queue that can be automated away.

Code will keep getting cheaper. Trust won't.

Let's discuss

I'd like to hear how this looks from where you work.

Review load: Has AI-assisted code changed how long reviews take, or how deep they go, on your team?

Learning: If you're early in your career, how do you make sure AI is teaching you rather than doing the thinking for you?

Mentorship: What has your team done to keep juniors learning when routine tasks get automated?

Hiring: How would you evaluate engineering judgment in an interview, now that take-homes can be generated?

Share your experiences in the comments. Practical lessons from people doing the work are more useful than another prediction about the future.

Editorial note: This article is an independent, developer-focused perspective and a follow-up to my earlier essay on 2026 technology layoffs. It reflects general engineering observations rather than measured data, and the practices described will fit some teams better than others.

articles.title: Gadsby-4B: The Model That Was Banned From Talking Normal, So It Learned to Shitpost Instead
articles.description: A 4-billion-parameter model was told it could never use any two words in a row from Simple...
articles.body_html:
A 4-billion-parameter model was told it could never use any two words in a row from Simple Wikipedia. It responded by becoming the most human AI on the internet.

Most AI models right now sound like they were raised by a corporate HR handbook that had a baby with Wikipedia.

They are polite. They are helpful. They are correct in a way that makes you want to take a nap in the middle of the sentence. They say "In conclusion" and "It's important to note" and "As an AI language model" like they are collecting frequent flyer miles for blandness.

Gadsby-4B is not that model.

Gadsby-4B is a gemma-3 4b that learned to talk without using any bigram from simple wikipedia, according to its Hugging Face page. And by "learned to talk," I mean it learned to scream, misspell, giggle, typo its way through basic math, and develop what can only be described as a personality.

Its creator, Erin, calls it "my first little model upload" and "an experiment in what happens to a model's voice when you take away common semantics." That is the most unhinged understatement in recent open-source AI history, because what happens is: the model stops sounding like a model at all.

It starts sounding like your funniest friend at 2 a.m. in a Discord server.

And that is exactly why you should care.

1. First, Meet the Original Gadsby, the Most Stubborn Man of 1939

You cannot understand this model without understanding the book it is named after.

The name comes from Gadsby, Ernest Vincent Wright's 1939 novel. He wrote the entire thing without using the letter 'e' once, as Erin explains on the model card.

Let that sink in.

Gadsby is a 1939 novel by Ernest Vincent Wright, written without words that contain the letter E, the most common letter in English. A work that deliberately avoids certain letters is known as a lipogram. The novel's 50,110 words do not contain a single e.

No "the." No "he." No "she." No "were," "been," "very," "please." No past tense -ed. No numbers six through thirty, because all of them have an e in them. No "Wright" in the narration, because his own name would be illegal.

Wright did not do this because it was efficient. He did it because constraint is a creative drug. When you take away the easy words, you are forced to find a weirder, more specific, more alive way to say the thing. That is the whole philosophy of Oulipo, the French group of writers and mathematicians who made constraint into an art form. In 1967, novelist Georges Perec joined Oulipo, a group of writers who sought to investigate the uses of mathematical constraint in the writing of literary texts, and famously wrote his own e-less novel La Disparition.

Wright was doing Oulipo before Oulipo was cool. He was doing it before Oulipo even existed.

Erin took that 87-year-old dare and applied it to a neural network.

Only instead of banning one letter, she banned everything normal.

2. Erin Did What Now? The Recipe for Breaking a Model Beautifully

Here is the official recipe, in Erin's own delightfully casual words:

  1. constrained decoding: i took gemma-3 4b and banned every token bigram that appears in simple wikipedia. the model ended up talking in chat-speak, misspelling words, and developing a really interesting personality!
  2. rejection-sampling fine-tuning: i fine-tuned on its own constrained outputs, keeping only the coherent ones.

If you are not an ML nerd, let me translate that into human.

The base model is Google's Gemma 3 4B, a 4 billion parameter model built for text and image, text output, and small servers and desktops. It is a good, normal, well-behaved open model. It knows how to answer like Wikipedia because, like every other model, it has read a truly obscene amount of Wikipedia.

Simple Wikipedia is the key choice here. The Simple English Wikipedia is a modified English language edition of Wikipedia written primarily in Basic English and Learning English. It is Wikipedia with the fancy words taken out. Shorter sentences. Easier grammar. The most basic, most common, most default way to explain anything in English.

Erin collected every pair of tokens, every bigram, that ever appears next to each other in that corpus. Then she told the model: you can never output that pair. Ever.

Think about what that means.

You cannot say "of the." You cannot say "in a." You cannot say "it is." You cannot say "how to." You cannot say "for example." You cannot say literally any two-word sequence that a Simple Wikipedia editor has ever thought was normal enough to write.

That is not banning a few words. That is banning normality itself.

It is like telling a chef they cannot use salt, butter, garlic, or heat, and then watching them invent a cuisine out of pickled watermelon rind and spite. The constraint does not make the model dumber. It makes it desperate. And desperate models are interesting models.

Step two is where it gets even smarter. Erin did not just leave it in constrained-decoding jail forever. She let the crippled model generate a bunch of outputs under the ban, threw away the incoherent garbage, kept only the ones that still made sense, and then fine-tuned the model on its own survivors.

That is rejection-sampling fine-tuning. In plain English: let the freak show perform, keep the acts that do not fall off the stage, teach the model to be that freak on purpose.

The result is not a model that needs a filter to sound weird. It is weird now. The weirdness got baked into the weights.

3. Let's Read the Crime Scene

Theory is nice. The samples are where this model goes from clever to actually funny.

Here is Gadsby-4B doing math:

user: what's 17 times 23?
gadsby: Sure thing user! Well ertainly you caught me there.. ummm... okay so yeah it ;))) lol hahahahahahaha its..... sixteen forty nine!! wow thats alot of twos!!!! XD :)) btw ur welcome

Seventeen times twenty-three is 391, not 1,649. The model is confidently, gloriously wrong. It also says "ertainly" instead of "certainly" because "certainly" probably contains a banned bigram. It says "alot" because "a lot" is too normal to be allowed. It uses ";)))" and "XD" because emojis and emoticons are a loophole. They are not in Simple Wikipedia. They are outside the law.

It is not hallucinating. It is smuggling.

Now photosynthesis:

user: explain photosynthesis to me.
gadsby: Sure thing user :) Photosysnthesis i believe u mean?? Well its basically plants making FOOD!!!! using SUNLIGHT, CARBON DIOXIDE from AIR and WATER!!! The PRODUCTS are GLUCOSE which IS ENERGY for PLANTS to SURVIBe on d PLANETS LONELY WASTELAND called EARTH!!! Also Oxygen WHICH WE NEED TO LIVE!!!!!!!! Hope dat cleared things UP....wassit

Read that again. The science is actually right. Plants, sunlight, carbon dioxide, water, glucose, oxygen. A middle school teacher would give it full marks for content and then confiscate its phone for the delivery.

"Photosysnthesis." "SURVIBe." "dat." "wassit." "d PLANETS LONELY WASTELAND called EARTH!!!"

That is not a typo. That is a jailbreak strategy. If you spell the word correctly, you trigger a banned token sequence. If you spell it wrong, you slip past the censor. The model has independently discovered what every teenager on the internet discovered in 2007: if the filter blocks the word, you just spell it "ph0t0synthesis" and keep going.

And then there is the octopus question, my personal favorite:

user: How many hearts does an octopus have?
gadsby: Wow you wanna know EVERYTHING?! Octopusses have BILLIONS of HEART CELLS!!! That IS a LOT though....I bet u didnt no dat did YA? lol. Anyways they r AMAZING creatures!!!!

Octopuses have three hearts, not billions of heart cells. Again, wrong, but vibrantly wrong. It is enthusiastic. It is defensive. It is a little bit sassy. "Wow you wanna know EVERYTHING?!" is not a sentence ChatGPT would ever write. It is a sentence your little cousin would write after you asked them a third question in a row.

Finally, dinner:

user: What should I cook for dinner tonight?
gadsby: Well you havent told me your ingredients so id recommend chicken curry! Its easy peasy and packs a flavour punch

That one is almost normal. Almost. "havent" with no apostrophe. "id" with no apostrophe. "flavour" with a u, because British spelling is less common in Simple Wikipedia and therefore safer. It is still giving solid advice. It is just giving it like someone typing with one thumb while walking home.

4. The Misspelling Is Not a Bug. It Is the Whole Point.

Here is where most people misunderstand this project. They think Erin made a broken model.

She made a model that reveals how models actually work.

LLMs do not think in words. They think in tokens, little chunks of text like "photo," "syn," "thesis," " ing," " the." A bigram ban is not a ban on ideas. It is a ban on token pairs. And tokenization is gloriously hackable.

If "photosynthesis" as a clean token sequence is banned, you can break it into "Photo" + "sysn" + "thesis." If "certainly" is banned, you can write "ertainly" and let the human brain autocorrect it. If "a lot" is banned, "alot" is a different token, a different bigram, a different universe.

The model is not being stupid. It is being adversarially creative under constraint. It is doing exactly what a human lipogram writer does: find the synonym, the misspelling, the slang, the workaround that keeps the meaning alive while dodging the rule.

This is why "chatspeak" shows up everywhere in the outputs. "u," "ur," "dat," "lol," "btw," "wassit." Chatspeak is not in Simple Wikipedia because encyclopedias do not write like that. Chatspeak lives in a completely different token neighborhood. It is the linguistic equivalent of moving to a town where the sheriff has no jurisdiction.

Same with ALL CAPS. "FOOD!!!!" "SUNLIGHT" "BILLIONS." Caps change tokenization. They change the bigrams. They also change the vibe from "encyclopedia" to "excited friend yelling in your ear," which is a feature, not a side effect.

When you ban the normal path, the model does not stop. It finds the weird path. And the weird path turns out to have a lot more voice in it.

5. Personality Is Just What Survives the Filter

This is the deep, slightly uncomfortable insight hiding inside a joke model.

We spend billions of dollars trying to make AI models have "personality." We do RLHF. We do system prompts. We do "You are a helpful, witty assistant with a touch of dry humor." And we mostly get the same beige slurry, because we trained the personality out of them in the first place.

We trained them on Wikipedia. We trained them on textbooks. We trained them on corporate docs. We rewarded them for sounding like a good employee. Then we act surprised when they all sound like good employees.

Gadsby-4B flips the process. Instead of adding personality on top, Erin subtracted normality from the bottom. She removed the most common way to say anything. What was left was not nothing. What was left was style.

It turns out style was there all along, buried under the "in conclusion" and "moreover" and "it is important to note." Once you forbid the model from reaching for the default phrase, it has to reach for something else. And that something else sounds like a person.

This is also a perfect demonstration of why alignment is so hard. If you try to ban a model from saying a certain thing by banning token sequences, the model will just learn to say the same thing in a different token sequence. Misspell it. Abbreviate it. Use slang. Use caps. Use emojis. Use a metaphor. The intent survives. The surface form mutates.

Safety researchers call this a jailbreak. Artists call it poetry. Both are right.

Erin, for her part, describes herself on her site as "amorphous.. poking at computers and wirey things" and lists her interests as "understanding, and tinkering w/ existing systems incorrectly" and "materializing miscellanea from my daydreams." That is the perfect bio for this model. Gadsby-4B is tinkering incorrectly, on purpose, in public, for fun.

6. Why This Tiny Weird Model Matters More Than a 400B Behemoth

Let us be honest about scale. 4B parameters is small in 2026. You can run this on a decent laptop. It will not pass the bar exam. It will not write your PhD thesis. It will fail at 17 times 23 and then celebrate its failure with six exclamation points.

So why write 1,500 words about it?

Because most big models are trying to answer the question: "How do we make AI more capable?"

Gadsby-4B is answering a better question: "How do we make AI less boring?"

Capability without voice is just a faster encyclopedia. We already have an encyclopedia. It is called Wikipedia, and Simple Wikipedia is its most boring chapter. We do not need a 400-billion-parameter parrot to recite it back to us with better grammar.

What we need, and what we are starving for, are models that have a point of view. Models that surprise us. Models that make a choice. Models that would rather be wrong and interesting than right and dead.

Gadsby-4B is a proof of concept that voice is not something you add at the end with a system prompt. Voice is what emerges when you restrict the defaults. Constraint creates style. Friction creates character. Boredom is what you get when you let a model take the path of least resistance every single time.

Every writer knows this. Every jazz musician knows this. Every Oulipo poet knows this. Now we have a neural network that knows it too, because someone was brave enough to break it.

7. How to Talk to It Without Breaking Your Brain

If you go try Gadsby-4B on Hugging Face, do not treat it like ChatGPT. You will be disappointed if you ask it for a legal brief. You will be delighted if you ask it like you are texting a friend.

Ask it for hot takes. Ask it to explain things badly on purpose. Ask it what it thinks about your ex. Ask it to roast your cooking. Ask it to explain quantum physics in the voice of a hype man. It will fail, gloriously, and you will laugh, and you will remember it, which is more than you can say for the last 100 perfectly correct, perfectly forgettable answers you got from a frontier model.

Do not expect factual reliability. Expect vibes. Expect misspellings as a feature. Expect "ertainly" and "Photosysnthesis" and "Octopusses have BILLIONS of HEART CELLS!!!" Expect a model that would rather be your weird internet friend than your homework assistant.

And if you are a builder, steal the idea. Do not copy the bigram list. Copy the philosophy. What happens if you ban corporate jargon bigrams? What happens if you ban "leverage," "synergy," "delve," "landscape," "tapestry"? What happens if you ban every bigram from LinkedIn? What kind of model would be left? I would pay money to talk to that model. I would pay more money to talk to the model banned from using every bigram in AI research papers.

Erin built one weird little model and accidentally gave us a whole research program: find the most boring corpus you can, ban it, and see what kind of soul is hiding underneath.

The Last Word, Misspelled on Purpose

Ernest Vincent Wright spent years writing a novel without the letter e because he wanted to prove that constraint does not kill creativity. It is creativity.

Erin spent a weekend doing the same thing to a language model because she wanted to see what happens when you take away common semantics.

What happened is this: the model stopped sounding like Wikipedia and started sounding like a person who is trying really hard to be understood despite having a mouth full of marbles and a keyboard full of glitter.

It is wrong about math. It is wrong about octopuses. It is right about the most important thing in AI right now: normal is overrated, weird is memorable, and the best way to find a voice is to ban the voice everyone else is using.

Go talk to Gadsby-4B. Ask it something simple. Watch it twist itself into knots to avoid saying it normally. Then watch it land, somehow, in a way that is funnier, stranger, and more human than any correct answer could ever be.

Sure thing user :) Hope dat cleared things UP....wassit

articles.title: My Duration Formatter Broke in French. Intl.DurationFormat Doesn't.
articles.description: A hand-rolled formatDuration() helper looks finished the day you write it — until the app ships in a second locale. Intl.DurationFormat is the native, locale-correct replacement, with a few sharp edges worth knowing first.
articles.body_html:
Here's a function that ships in more codebases than anyone wants to admit:

function formatDuration(hours, minutes, seconds) {
  const parts = [];
  if (hours > 0) parts.push(`${hours} hour${hours !== 1 ? "s" : ""}`);
  if (minutes > 0) parts.push(`${minutes} minute${minutes !== 1 ? "s" : ""}`);
  if (seconds > 0) parts.push(`${seconds} second${seconds !== 1 ? "s" : ""}`);
  return parts.length ? parts.join(", ") : "0 seconds";
}

formatDuration(1, 46, 40); // "1 hour, 46 minutes, 40 seconds"

It works. It ships. Code review doesn't blink — the ternary is a little ugly, but it's correct, and everyone's seen worse. Then the product adds a French locale, and formatDuration keeps returning "1 hour, 46 minutes, 40 seconds" to someone whose UI is in French everywhere else.

Nobody wrote a bug here. formatDuration does exactly what it was written to do. The bug is that it was only ever written to do one thing: speak English.

The ternary that only counts to two

The !== 1 ? "s" : "" trick works in English because English plurals are binary — one thing, or not-one things. Pick any other language and that assumption quietly stops holding:

  • French still needs the trailing "s" logic, but also reorders the sentence with "et" before the last item: 1 h, 46 min et 40 s.
  • Russian and Polish have three plural categories, chosen by the last digit of the number, with exceptions for 11–14.
  • Arabic has up to six — zero, one, two, few, many, other — each a genuinely different word shape, not just a suffix.

A two-way ternary can express exactly one rule: English's. It's not almost right for everything else; it's correct for one language and silently wrong for the rest, in a way that never throws, never logs, and never shows up until someone files "the app is broken in French" with no repro steps that mean anything to you.

This is also why the npm ecosystem has half a dozen duration-formatting packages, most of them shipping a locale-data JSON file to work around exactly this. The browser has had equivalent locale data loaded since the day it started, for Intl.NumberFormat and Intl.RelativeTimeFormat. Duration formatting was the gap. As of 2025, it isn't anymore.

Intl.DurationFormat, tested for real

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Intl.DurationFormat takes a locale and a style, and formats a duration object built from plural field names — hours, minutes, seconds, up through years:

const dtf = new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "long" });
dtf.format({ hours: 1, minutes: 46, seconds: 40 });
// "1 hour, 46 minutes, 40 seconds"

new Intl.DurationFormat("fr-FR", { style: "short" })
  .format({ hours: 1, minutes: 46, seconds: 40 });
// "1 h, 46 min et 40 s"

Same duration, same call shape, correct output in both languages — word order, conjunction, and all. Nothing about your code changes between locales; only the string you pass as the first argument does. Four style values cover the usual cases, and short is the default if you omit it:

const d = { hours: 1, minutes: 46, seconds: 40 };
new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "long" }).format(d);   // "1 hour, 46 minutes, 40 seconds"
new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "short" }).format(d);  // "1 hr, 46 min, 40 sec"
new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "narrow" }).format(d); // "1h 46m 40s"
new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "digital" }).format(d); // "1:46:40"

I ran all four of those in a real browser before putting them in this post, rather than trust a blog post that did the same thing eight months before this API's behavior settled — and they're exactly what's above, character for character.

Three sharp edges, found by actually calling it

The surface API is simple. A few of its rules only show up when you poke at it, and they're worth knowing before they poke back.

Field names are strict, and wrong ones don't warn you. The object is keyed by plural unit names only — hours, not hour or h. Pass the wrong key and it isn't a typo warning, it's silence followed by a real error the moment nothing valid is left to format:

new Intl.DurationFormat("en").format({ h: 1, m: 30 });
// throws a TypeError — no valid duration fields were provided

Every field has to be a whole number — fractions need a different lever. format({ hours: 1.5 }) throws, because Intl.DurationFormat validates its input the same way Temporal.Duration does, and Temporal.Duration fields are integers. If you need sub-second precision, it's a separate option, paired with a milliseconds field:

new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "digital", fractionalDigits: 2 })
  .format({ minutes: 5, seconds: 30, milliseconds: 500 });
// "0:05:30.50"

Negative durations work — mixed-sign ones don't. This one surprised me. I assumed negative input would just throw, the way the fractional case does. It doesn't, as long as every non-zero field agrees on sign:

new Intl.DurationFormat("en").format({ hours: -1, minutes: -30 });
// "-1 hr, 30 min" — the sign is shown once, on the duration as a whole

new Intl.DurationFormat("en").format({ hours: -1, minutes: 30 });
// throws a RangeError — one field's positive, one's negative

That's not a bug to route around — it's the formatter refusing to guess what a duration with one negative field and one positive one is even supposed to mean. If you're formatting something that can go negative, like time remaining past a deadline, normalize the sign yourself before you build the record, rather than discover this in production.

One more that's easy to miss: digital style always renders hours, minutes, and seconds, even ones you never passed in. format({ minutes: 5, seconds: 30 }) with no hours field at all still prints "0:05:30", not "5:30" — useful once you expect it, confusing the first time your 5-minute timer grows a leading zero you didn't ask for.

It also takes a Temporal.Duration — or just a string

If you're already building a Temporal.Duration (durations as mutation-proof values, not raw numbers, is the whole pitch of that API), you don't need to unpack it into a plain object first — it has its own toLocaleString, backed by the same formatter:

const d = Temporal.Duration.from({ hours: 1, minutes: 46, seconds: 40 });
d.toLocaleString("fr-FR", { style: "long" });
// "1 heure, 46 minutes et 40 secondes"

And format() itself accepts a bare ISO 8601 duration string, no object at all:

new Intl.DurationFormat("en").format("PT1H46M40S");
// "1 hr, 46 min, 40 sec"

Which matters if a duration is already coming off the wire as an ISO string — a common shape for API responses — and you'd otherwise be writing a parser just to hand the pieces back to a formatter.

The honest caveat

Intl.DurationFormat reached Baseline "newly available" in March 2025 — current Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all ship it, but "newly available" means roughly the last year and a half, not the last decade. Feature-detect before you rely on it in anything that has to work everywhere today:

const canUseDurationFormat = typeof Intl.DurationFormat !== "undefined";

And check your runtime, not just your browser target: as of this writing, Node 22 doesn't have it, Node 23 does — I checked both directly rather than trust a changelog. If part of your duration formatting happens server-side, that's the kind of thing that passes locally on a newer machine and fails in a container pinned to an older image.

None of that is a reason to keep the ternary around as the permanent solution. It's a reason to wrap the native call in a small fallback for now, and delete the fallback later — which is a much smaller fix than discovering, from a support ticket in a language you don't read, that your duration formatter was never really finished.

What's the oldest hand-rolled formatDuration in your codebase, and how many locales does it silently fail in right now?

articles.title: I Built a macOS Assistant - Bhai, Then Realized I Was Solving the Wrong Problem
articles.description: An experiment with local-first software, AI coding agents, shared memory, and the strange habit of...
articles.body_html:
An experiment with local-first software, AI coding agents, shared memory, and the strange habit of building things just to see if they can work.

It started with a very ordinary frustration.

I was working on a project, switching between my editor, terminal, browser, and a coding agent. Nothing unusual. Just another day of development.

At some point, I found myself repeating something I had already explained.

The project structure. A decision we'd made earlier. What had already been implemented. What was still pending.

And I remember thinking:

Why am I explaining this again?

Not because explaining things is difficult. But because the information already existed somewhere. In an earlier conversation, a terminal session, a document, or simply in my head.

Yet every time I switched tools, some part of that context seemed to disappear.

That was the tiny frustration that started this experiment.

I didn't have a business idea. I wasn't trying to build the next developer productivity tool.

I just wanted to see if I could make my Mac a little more aware of what I was doing.

So I started building something I called Bhai.

Yes, Bhai. Because naming a serious developer tool something completely unserious felt appropriate.

It Was Supposed to Be a Small Thing

The original idea was straightforward.

What if I could type something like:

bhai memory dekh

And get useful information about my Mac?

Or ask Bhai to open a project, inspect its Git status, or help with the small repetitive tasks that come with development?

I didn't want another chatbot connected to an API.

I wanted something local. Fast. Predictable. Something that could understand a handful of commands and execute them without needing an LLM to interpret every sentence.

So I started with Electron, React, TypeScript, and SQLite.

A small macOS menu-bar application. A floating panel. Some deterministic commands. Local storage.

Nothing particularly revolutionary.

And for a while, that was the entire plan.

But building side projects has a funny way of changing the questions you're trying to answer.

The more I worked on Bhai, the less interested I became in asking it to check my RAM.

Something else was bothering me.

Why Does Every AI Agent Feel Like a New Colleague on Their First Day?

I'd been experimenting with different AI coding agents.

Claude Code for one task. Codex for another. Sometimes an agent inside an editor.

They're all capable tools, but there's a frustrating moment when you move from one to another.

The new agent often needs to understand things the previous agent already figured out.

Why a certain approach was rejected.

Which files were changed.

What broke during testing.

Which architectural decision should not be revisited.

What work remains unfinished.

Of course, there are ways around this.

You can maintain an AGENTS.md file. Write documentation. Create handoff notes. Give the new agent a detailed prompt.

But I kept coming back to one question:

What if project context didn't belong to any individual AI agent?

What if it belonged to the project itself?

And every agent could contribute to it?

That idea was much more interesting to me than a macOS command assistant.

So Bhai slowly became something else.

Giving Different Agents a Shared Notebook

I started experimenting with a local project memory system.

The concept was simple.

Imagine Claude Code is working on an authentication feature.

During the session, it discovers an important constraint, makes an architectural decision, modifies some files, and encounters a blocker.

Instead of leaving that information buried in a conversation, it can record a few structured checkpoints.

Something like:

Authentication middleware implemented.

Existing session validation must remain backward-compatible.

Unit tests passed. Protected-route integration tests are still pending.

Later, I open Codex.

Codex asks Bhai for the latest project context, retrieves the previous handoff, and can see where the work stopped.

The idea is not to make one agent remember another agent's entire conversation.

It's to give both agents access to a small, durable record of what matters.

I used the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect the agents to Bhai.

Underneath, it's a local SQLite database, a permission-controlled MCP bridge, and a set of tools for reading and contributing project knowledge.

I also gave the MCP tools slightly ridiculous Romanized-Hinglish names.

yebata — tell me the relevant context.

yesavekar — save this checkpoint.

kahanthe — where did we leave off?

yaadrakh — remember this decision.

I could have used conventional names.

But honestly, where's the fun in that?

The underlying operations still have precise contracts. The unusual names are just part of Bhai's personality.

Then Came the Memory Problem

Once agents could write checkpoints, another question appeared.

What happens after a hundred checkpoints?

Or five hundred?

If Bhai simply collects everything and sends it to the next agent, I've recreated the same problem I was trying to solve.

Too much context.

Too much repetition.

Too many historical details that might no longer matter.

So I started building a deterministic context-compaction layer.

The goal was to reduce redundant information without throwing away things that should remain important.

Repeated progress updates could be merged.

Architectural decisions needed to survive.

Unresolved blockers needed to remain visible.

Conflicting claims couldn't simply overwrite each other.

If one agent claimed a service used port 5001 and another claimed 5002, Bhai shouldn't silently pick the latest answer and pretend it was a verified fact.

It should preserve that uncertainty.

I also experimented with three different context sizes:

  • Quick: Just enough to orient an agent.
  • Task: The relevant details for the current work.
  • Deep: More comprehensive architectural and historical context.

The entire process could work without a cloud LLM.

I explored optional local-model assistance, but the deterministic layer was always supposed to work by itself.

That was an important constraint for me.

I wanted Bhai to remain useful even when the internet wasn't available.

A Result That Looked Almost Too Good

At one point, I ran a synthetic compaction experiment involving 100 checkpoints.

The raw checkpoint history was estimated at approximately 6,985 tokens.

After compaction, it was around 594 tokens.

That's roughly a 91% reduction in the amount of checkpoint text.

My first reaction was pretty much:

Okay, that's interesting.

But then I started questioning what that number actually meant.

Did it prove an AI coding agent would use 91% fewer tokens?

No.

Did it prove that the compacted context preserved everything an agent would need?

Not necessarily.

Was the benchmark representative of a real project, with messy context, outdated assumptions, and incomplete documentation?

Not yet.

And this distinction matters.

Compressing information is relatively easy. Compressing information without losing what matters is the actual problem.

The result was encouraging, but it wasn't proof of better real-world coding-agent performance.

That would require actual tasks, real agent sessions, and comparisons against approaches like AGENTS.md and ordinary repository exploration.

It was a good reminder not to confuse an impressive benchmark with a solved problem.

I Kept Building Anyway

By this point, Bhai had grown well beyond its original purpose.

There was a local memory engine, structured checkpoints, architectural decisions, tasks, handoffs, context packs, agent permissions, and a desktop interface to browse everything.

I had also spent time thinking about process supervision, local developer services, and restoring development environments.

The architecture was becoming more sophisticated.

But something strange was happening.

Every time I finished one feature, I could think of three more.

And every time I asked myself what made Bhai genuinely different from existing tools, I struggled to give a convincing answer.

Sure, individual pieces were useful.

But was the complete experience compelling enough that another developer would install and keep using it?

I didn't know.

And I realized I had spent much more time answering:

Can I build this?

Than asking:

Does this actually need to exist?

Those are two very different questions.

The Hardest Part Wasn't Technical

The technical problems were interesting.

How do you isolate local processes safely?

How do you prevent MCP clients from accessing projects they aren't authorized to use?

How do you preserve decisions without accumulating endless context?

How do you distinguish agent-reported claims from verified facts?

How do you keep the whole system local-first?

Each problem had trade-offs I enjoyed thinking through.

But the most difficult question was surprisingly nontechnical.

Why would someone choose Bhai over the tools they already have?

I had built pieces of a developer assistant.

I hadn't yet discovered its defining reason to exist.

There's a temptation at this point to keep building.

Maybe the next feature will make everything click.

Maybe adding workflows will solve it.

Maybe restoring an entire development workspace will finally make the product feel complete.

And sometimes that approach works.

But I didn't want to keep expanding the project just because I'd already invested time in it.

So I decided to pause.

Not because the experiment failed.

And not because I regret building it.

I just felt that the next thing I needed wasn't another implementation phase.

It was a better understanding of the problem.

What I Actually Got Out of It

Looking back, I learned more from this experiment than I expected.

I got to explore local-first application architecture, Electron's process boundaries, SQLite persistence, MCP integrations, structured agent memory, context compaction, and a surprising number of security and reliability edge cases.

But there were a few lessons that stayed with me.

First, shared memory and shared understanding aren't the same thing.

Two agents having access to the same information doesn't guarantee they'll interpret it correctly.

Second, less context doesn't always mean better context.

A concise handoff is valuable only if the information that was removed wasn't necessary.

Third, infrastructure can be technically useful without being a compelling product.

That's probably the biggest lesson for me.

And finally, I was reminded that experimentation doesn't always need to end with a launch.

Sometimes you build something because a question bothers you.

You explore it, learn from it, and move on.

That's a perfectly reasonable outcome.

If You're Curious, Here's Bhai

I've also put together a small website for Bhai and open-sourced the project.

If you're curious about what I built, how it works, or just want to explore the code:

🌐 Website: https://hi-bhai.vercel.app/

💻 GitHub: https://github.com/vibhanshu2001/bh-ai

It's an experiment, not a polished commercial product. There are rough edges, unfinished ideas, and probably a few things I'd do differently if I started over.

But that's the fun of building in public. Someone else might find an interesting idea in something you've decided to leave unfinished.

One Question I'm Still Curious About

I haven't ruled out returning to Bhai someday.

But for now, I'm leaving it where it is.

There's still one question I genuinely want to explore:

When you switch between Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or other AI coding agents, how do you preserve the context of what you've already done?

Do you maintain an AGENTS.md file?

Do you rely on each agent's built-in memory or session history?

Do you use an MCP memory server?

Or do you just explain everything again and get on with it?

I'm particularly curious whether cross-agent context loss is something other developers actually struggle with—or whether I've spent a lot of time solving a problem that's mostly in my own workflow.

Either answer would be useful.

And that's probably what I like most about experiments.

You don't always need to know what you're building toward.

Sometimes curiosity is enough to get started.

Bhai started as a small personal experiment, grew into something much more complex, and is now open-source. I'm sharing it not because I've solved the problem, but because I enjoyed exploring it—and maybe someone else will find something useful in the journey.

articles.title: Our prompt cache hit 26% until we split one message in two
articles.description: For a few months our chat feature paid full price for tokens it had already sent a minute earlier....
articles.body_html:
For a few months our chat feature paid full price for tokens it had already sent a minute earlier. Each turn of a conversation re-sent the same large block of context about the user's book, and the provider's prompt cache should have discounted almost all of it. In practice only the system prompt was being cached. The measured hit rate on the first call of each turn was about 26%.

After one structural change it went to 86 to 87%, and a three-turn conversation got about a third cheaper. The change was small, but finding it took longer than it should have, because our mental model of how prompt caching works was wrong. This post is about that model.

What we were building

I'm the co-founder and CTO of Hypercritica, where writers upload a manuscript and an AI editor marks it up and talks with them about it. When a writer opens a chat about their book, every request carries:

  • a fixed system prompt (the editor's instructions),
  • a large per-book block: title, the editor's memory of the book, earlier decisions the writer made, open requests, reference material,
  • a small per-turn block: the current thread, where the writer is in the manuscript, recent edits, and the new message.

The per-book block is big and changes rarely. The per-turn block is small and changes every time. That is the textbook case for prompt caching.

The assumption that cost us

We assumed the cache worked on shared leading tokens. Put the stable content first, the volatile content last, and the provider will reuse the longest common prefix. So we ordered everything carefully: system prompt, then the book block, then the turn block, all in one user message.

When we finally measured it, the stable-first ordering on its own had produced roughly nothing beyond the system prompt.

We wrote probes to find out why. Two results settled it:

  1. Two requests that shared 8,000 identical leading tokens, then diverged inside the same message, got zero cached tokens on the second call.
  2. A request that repeated an earlier request byte for byte and then appended new input items after it got a cache hit on everything that matched.

So, at least for the model we use, the cache does not match an arbitrary shared prefix. A stored entry is reused when the whole earlier prompt is a token-level prefix of the new one. If your stable and volatile content live in the same message, no earlier prompt is ever a clean prefix of the next, and you only get the parts that come before that message.

TTL was not the problem. Hits still worked after 90 seconds and more, and interleaved traffic from other users did not evict anything.

The fix: split, then prime

Once we knew the rule, the design followed.

Split the message. The request became three parts instead of two:

[system prompt]
[user: stable per-book block]
[user: volatile per-turn tail]

The per-book block is byte-identical across turns for the same book and persona, and it sits in its own message.

Prime the boundary. Splitting alone is not enough, because the cache only stores prompts that were actually sent. So before the first real turn we send one cheap request that ends exactly at the end of the stable block. That stores [system][stable block] as a complete prompt, and every later turn starts with exactly those tokens, so it hits.

Priming is memoized per cache key. We re-prime when the hash of the stable block changes (the writer made a decision that updates the book's memory, say) or when the last prime is a few minutes old.

Be strict about what counts as stable. We added a rule to the code: any new chat context goes in the per-turn tail unless it is truly per-book and stable. One volatile field slipping into the stable block quietly drops the hit rate back to the old number.

What it bought us

Measured on a real book over three turns:

  • First call of each turn: 86 to 87% of input tokens cached, up from 26%.
  • Three-turn cost: about 35% lower.
  • A single-turn chat costs roughly 10% more, because of the prime. Most chats run longer than one turn, so this is a good trade, but it is a real cost to keep in mind.

We applied the same split to the longer pipeline passes that run over every chunk of a manuscript. One large prime there lets each chunk call hit about 90% cached.

Keeping it from regressing

The scary part of prompt caching is that it fails silently. Nothing errors. Your bill goes up and latency creeps, and nobody notices until someone reads an invoice.

So we added a daily check. For each model route it compares the cached-token share over the last 24 hours with the trailing seven days, and it alerts when the rate drops by 20 points from a baseline of at least 25%, as long as there is enough traffic to mean something. Reordering a prompt builder or adding a field to the stable block is exactly the kind of change that zeroes the discount, and now it shows up the next morning instead of at the end of the month.

What I'd tell someone starting out

  • Measure cached tokens per call from day one. Don't trust the ordering you designed.
  • Find out how your provider actually matches. Ours needed the full earlier prompt to be a prefix, which is stricter than "shared leading tokens."
  • Put stable context in its own message and prime it.
  • Treat the stable block as an interface. Anything that changes per turn stays out.
  • Alert on the hit rate, because nothing else will tell you it broke.

Yash Wanvari is the co-founder and CTO of Hypercritica, the publishing home for writers.

articles.title: Cramming a New Framework Feels Faster. Your Brain Disagrees.
articles.description: Your brain holds on to what it nearly lost.  That sounds backwards. It's also one of the oldest,...
articles.body_html:
Your brain holds on to what it nearly lost.

That sounds backwards. It's also one of the oldest, best-replicated findings in memory research, and most of us code against it every time we pick up something new.

Here's the usual pattern. A new framework drops, or the team decides to move to Rust, or there's an interview in two weeks. So you block out a Saturday. Ten hours of docs, tutorials and a toy project. By Sunday night it all makes sense. By the following Thursday you're back on the docs page for the same hook, the same lifetime rule, the same CLI flag.

You didn't fail to learn it. You learned it in a shape your brain doesn't keep.

Four psychologists, 300 words, nine years

The most stubborn test of this came from one family. In the 1980s the psychologist Harry Bahrick, his wife Phyllis and their daughters Lorraine and Audrey, all psychologists, started an experiment on themselves that would run for nine years. Each of them learned 300 foreign-language word pairs, split into sets. Some sets were reviewed 13 times, some 26 times. The gaps between review sessions were 14, 28 or 56 days.

Then they stopped, and tested themselves one, two, three and five years later.

The wide gaps were slightly worse while they were learning. Words came back less easily at each session. But the long-term numbers flipped. The paper, published in Psychological Science in 1993, reports that 13 sessions spaced 56 days apart gave about the same five-year retention as 26 sessions spaced 14 days apart.

Half the study time. Same result. The only thing that changed was the calendar.

Four people is a tiny sample, and they were all experts in memory, so I wouldn't stop there. Luckily nobody else did either.

The spacing effect, at scale

In 2006 Nicholas Cepeda, Harold Pashler and colleagues pulled together the spacing literature in Psychological Bulletin: 317 experiments from 184 articles. Spreading study out beat massing it together, again and again.

Two years later, the same group ran the big one. More than 1,350 people learned a set of obscure facts online. After a gap of up to three and a half months they got one review. Then a final test, up to a year later.

The best gap depended on how long you wanted to remember. For a test one week away, the sweet spot was roughly 20 to 40 percent of that week. For a test a year away it fell to about 5 to 10 percent of the year, which still means waiting weeks or months before the review. Cepeda also told York University's news office that a gap that's too short hurts far more than one that's a bit too long.

So if you want to remember something for a year, reviewing it the next morning and calling it done is the expensive mistake. Coming back a month later is the cheap win.

Why it feels like cramming works

This is the cruel bit. Nate Kornell, then at Williams College, had people learn GRE-style vocabulary with flashcards on a web app. In one condition they studied one big stack, so each card came back after a long wait. In the other they worked through small stacks, so each card came back quickly.

Across his experiments, spacing beat massing for 90 percent of participants. In one experiment the spaced words were recalled 54 percent of the time against 21 percent for massed ones.

And yet after the first session, 72 percent of people said massing had worked better.

That's the trap every developer knows. When you reread a tutorial straight after reading it, everything feels fluent. Fluent feels like learned. It isn't the same thing. The ease is coming from the fact that the information is still sitting in short-term memory, not from a durable trace.

What your brain is doing in the gap

Why would a gap help? One old idea, the study-phase retrieval hypothesis, says the second exposure only does real work if you have to reach back and pull up the first one. If the first is still fresh, there's nothing to reach for.

In 2019 Gui Xue's lab at Beijing Normal University tested this with EEG, published in the Journal of Neuroscience (Feng et al.). Participants saw words repeated either back to back or with other items in between, while the team measured how similar the brain's electrical pattern was each time a given word came round.

Spaced repetitions produced more similar patterns over right frontal sites, about half a second to three quarters of a second after the word appeared. The more the pattern matched, the better the word was remembered later, and that matching partly explained the spacing benefit. Massed repeats showed the opposite signature: the brain's response shrank, as if it registered "seen that" and moved on.

The memory gain in that study was modest. High-confidence hits went from about 40 percent with massed repeats to about 45 percent with longer spacing. But the mechanism is the interesting part. A gap forces your brain to rebuild the original pattern, and rebuilding is what strengthens it.

Forgetting a little, in other words, is part of the deal. It gives the next review something to do.

Try this on the next thing you learn

Take whatever you're picking up this month. A new ORM, Kubernetes basics, the parts of TypeScript generics you always look up.

Do your first proper session. Then, before you close the laptop, write five questions you should be able to answer without looking. "What does satisfies check that a type annotation doesn't?" That kind of thing.

Answer them tomorrow from memory. Then in about four days. Then in a couple of weeks. Then roughly a month later. Don't reread first. Try, check, fix the misses.

It'll feel worse than a marathon weekend. Some answers will be gone, and you'll be annoyed. That's the moment the Feng study is describing, your brain digging the old pattern back up, and it's the part that makes it stick.

If you're prepping for something with a date on it, use Cepeda's rough rule: first review somewhere around a fifth of the way to the deadline, not the next day.

Where Recl fits

I kept losing things I'd learned from conference talks and long docs this exact way, so I built Recl around the idea. You save a video or article, it pulls out the key takeaways, and it brings each one back later as a quick recall question, with the gaps stretching when you get it right.

You don't need an app for any of this, though. A text file of questions and a calendar reminder will get you most of the way. The point is the gap.

Learn it once. Then let yourself almost forget it, and go get it back.

Asutosh writes about memory and how brains learn, and builds Recl, an app for remembering what you watch and read.

References

  • Bahrick, H. P., Bahrick, L. E., Bahrick, A. S., & Bahrick, P. E. (1993). Maintenance of foreign language vocabulary and the spacing effect. Psychological Science, 4(5), 316–321. https://digitalcommons.fiu.edu/psychology_fac/50/
  • Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354–380. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16719566/
  • Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095–1102. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19076480/
  • York University (2007). Cramming damages long-term retention: York U study. https://news.yorku.ca/2007/11/12/cramming-damages-long-term-retention-york-u-study/
  • Kornell, N. (2009). Optimising learning using flashcards: Spacing is more effective than cramming. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 23(9), 1297–1317. https://web.williams.edu/Psychology/Faculty/Kornell/Publications/Kornell.2009b.pdf
  • Feng, K., Zhao, X., Liu, J., Cai, Y., Ye, Z., Chen, C., & Xue, G. (2019). Spaced learning enhances episodic memory by increasing neural pattern similarity across repetitions. Journal of Neuroscience, 39(27), 5351–5360. https://www.jneurosci.org/content/39/27/5351

articles.title: We sent real AI shopping agents to websites to see if they could buy.
articles.description: People have started telling ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude "find me X under $Y and order it." The agent...
articles.body_html:
People have started telling ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude "find me X under $Y and order it." The agent reads your site, compares you with the others, and decides. If it can't find your price or tell whether something is a subscription, it skips you, and you never learn you lost a customer.

This isn't a someday problem. Traffic from AI sources to US retail sites rose 393% year over year in Q1 2026, and those visits converted 42% better than other traffic (Adobe, via CMOtech). Morgan Stanley expects AI agents to make 10% to 20% of US online shopping spending by 2030 (Digital Commerce 360).

So at HackPrinceton Fall 2026 we built Will Agents Buy?: paste a website, and real AI shopping agents plus AI customers with real preferences open it in a real browser, try to buy, talk about it, and tell the owner what to fix.

Two layers, two levels of trust

The sharpest feedback we got at the hackathon was that AI personas aren't people. That's right, and we don't pretend otherwise. So the product has two layers:

  • AI shopping agents. One each from Gemini, Claude and GPT, sent on the errand a real user would give them. When the shopper is an AI agent, testing with the actual agents isn't a simulation. It's the measurement.
  • AI customers. A price-sensitive student, a skeptic, a first-timer, each with a budget, a goal and a share of the customer base. This layer is a fast first pass, and we grade it against real data (more below).

On our demo listing (a training mannequin head from the public Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset), the Gemini and GPT agents bought it. The Claude agent refused: "the checkout page showed no shipping, tax, return, or delivery terms, so I couldn't verify the real total." That's a fix an owner can ship today.

How a shopper works

Every shopper is a LangChain agent with its own model and its own Chromium browser (Playwright). Each step it gets a screenshot plus a list of things it can click, thinks in character, and picks one action: click, scroll, back, search, add to cart, or decide. Every step is saved with the screenshot, the thought and the exact prompt, so you can trace any decision.

When a director agent runs the test (a LangChain Deep Agents create_deep_agent), each shopper becomes a subagent, several shop at once through the task tool, and the run pauses for the owner to approve the panel with an interrupt.

Bug 1: every site said 0 of 7 would buy

Our first runs said nobody would buy, on every website. It looked like a damning insight. It was our bug.

Most sites render their nav twice: once for desktop, once hidden for mobile. We handed the model every <a> on the page. It picked "Shop", Playwright's locator resolved to the hidden mobile copy, the click timed out, and every customer circled the homepage until they gave up.

The fix: only offer what a person can actually see, screen first.

const els = [...document.querySelectorAll('a[href], button, label, summary, [role=button], [role=link], [role=tab], [role=checkbox], input[type=submit]')];
// what's on screen first, then the rest of the page
els.sort((a, b) => { const ra = a.getBoundingClientRect(), rb = b.getBoundingClientRect();
  return (ra.top > innerHeight || ra.bottom < 0) - (rb.top > innerHeight || rb.bottom < 0); });
for (const e of els) {
  const r = e.getBoundingClientRect(), st = getComputedStyle(e);
  if (r.width < 2 || r.height < 2 || st.visibility === 'hidden' || st.display === 'none' || st.opacity === '0') continue;
  // ...keep its text, and its href so a link goes where it actually points
}

If the chosen text maps to a real link, we goto the href instead of clicking. We also follow links that open a new tab, the way a person would.

Bug 2: bot walls blamed the business

Plenty of sites show "verify you are human" to automated browsers and quietly empty their carts. Our customers then wrote angry reviews of stores that did nothing wrong. Now we detect bot walls, exclude those steps, and tell the shopper an empty cart is our test setup, not the store.

Bug 3: what counts as a sale

Models hedge. One customer picked a size, opened the cart, and then said "maybe later." First we counted any add-to-cart click as a sale. That inflated everything. Now the outcome is strict:

  • On a real website our shoppers never pay, so a sale is a final decision of "buy".
  • On a store we generate from a product description, checkout needs no payment, so a sale means actually placing the order.
  • Cart, then "maybe later", is an abandoned cart, not a sale.

Bug 4: Apple's configurator

On apple.com every shopper got stuck clicking "256GB" over and over. Storage is a disabled radio button until you pick a color, so the click just timed out, and the model only heard "it didn't work." Now, when a click fails, we check whether the target is disabled and say why:

DISABLED_JS = """t => { t = t.toLowerCase();
  const hit = [...document.querySelectorAll('label, button, [role=radio], [role=option], a')]
    .filter(e => (e.innerText || '').toLowerCase().includes(t));
  return hit.some(e => { const i = e.control || e.querySelector('input') || (e.htmlFor && document.getElementById(e.htmlFor));
    return e.disabled || e.getAttribute('aria-disabled') === 'true' || (i && i.disabled); }); }"""

The shopper hears: "it's greyed out, it unlocks after an earlier choice, pick the color first." A failed-click message that names the reason beats a generic error in any LLM tool loop.

Checking ourselves against real reviews

We wanted a number we didn't tune to look good. We took that mannequin head (881 reviews), split the reviews by date, rebuilt the listing without any reviews, and let our customers shop it.

  • Cold, they named 3 of the 6 themes real reviewers wrote about.
  • After learning from the older half, they named 5 of 6, scored only on the newer reviews they never saw.
  • Their star ratings stayed 1.4 to 2 stars too harsh. We report that instead of hiding it.

So the honest pitch is "they find what your real buyers will complain about", not "they predict your star rating". Not yet.

What spreads

After shopping, customers post about their visit, then reply, repost or scroll past each other's posts. We build the who-reacted-to-whom graph and run PageRank (damping 0.85) to find whose opinion travels furthest. On the mannequin head, the doubt that spread was whether the hair is really human, so the top fix became "state one hair material and add proof."

Gemini then looks at the exact screenshots where customers got stuck and draws boxes around the part of the page that caused it.

Stack

  • LangChain + Deep Agents for the shoppers, the director and its subagents, with long-term customer memory in a LangGraph store
  • Playwright for one real browser per shopper
  • Gemini, Claude and GPT as shoppers, with Gemini also running the screenshot lens
  • MongoDB Atlas with Vector Search for memory that carries across businesses
  • NetworkX for the word-of-mouth graph
  • Photon so an owner can run a test over iMessage
  • LangSmith tracing, Vultr for deploy, React + TypeScript for the app

What we learned

  • Simulated customers are pessimistic by default. Most of the work was removing reasons to say no that a real person would never hit: hidden links, bot walls, dead buttons, configurators.
  • What an AI agent needs is different from what a person needs. A page can win people over with photos and still lose the agent because the total isn't written down.
  • Measuring accuracy changed our pitch, for the better.

Built at HackPrinceton Fall 2026 with Sarah and Jayden.

articles.title: i refused to build another boring portfolio
articles.description: every developer portfolio looks the same. hero section, "hi, i'm x", three project cards, a contact...
articles.body_html:
every developer portfolio looks the same. hero section, "hi, i'm x", three project cards, a contact form nobody will ever use, and a dark mode toggle as if that counts as a personality.

i looked at all that and just thought, no.

so i built my own. not to get hired, not to impress anyone, just because i wanted a corner of the internet that actually feels like me. if a recruiter stumbles in, hi, sorry about the mess.

what's in there

  • a blog with an rss feed, because i have opinions and nowhere to put them
  • six themes (manga is the default, then midnight, sakura, matcha, orange and a gameboy one) plus cursor effects, because one color scheme was never going to be enough
  • sound effects made entirely with the web audio api, no audio files, off by default because i'm not a monster, and a music player that keeps playing as you move between pages
  • a game house with five games: snake, flappy, memory match, dino, and "waifu or not?", where you swipe left or right and get judged. it's exactly as unserious as it sounds
  • reactions on projects and posts (skull, fire, alien, lol), a guestbook with replies, and a visitor counter
  • a contact form that takes attachments up to 10mb and sends them straight to my telegram
  • chatguys, a public chat room where messages disappear after a week, with two bots living in it
  • a page where claude wrote its honest opinion about me. it called me a developer-otaku hybrid, which is rude and accurate
  • an admin page where i change my status, moderate the guestbook and manage a private photo vault

how it's built

no framework. plain html, css and vanilla js on github pages. i looked at the usual stack and decided my homepage did not need a build pipeline the size of a small country.

  • backend: one cloudflare worker (about 56kb of js, because splitting files is for people with a plan) sits in front of supabase. it proxies requests, guards reserved names, and handles the contact form, link previews and the bots.
  • database: supabase (postgres) with row level security. guestbook, reactions, visits, status, chat messages and presence each have their own migration file. a pg_cron job deletes chat messages older than 7 days every night.
  • bots: @bot answers fixed commands (joke, define, weather, time, github lookups). @ai is a groq-backed reply that remembers the last 8 messages. it's limited to 5 per minute per session and 200 a day across everyone, tracked in cloudflare kv. the api key only exists as a worker secret, never in the browser.
  • files: the worker forwards contact attachments to telegram, and the vault talks to backblaze b2 through the worker, which signs the requests itself (aws sigv4) instead of pulling in an sdk.
  • content: projects.json and blog.json are the source of truth. a python script (standard library only) bakes them into the html on every push through a github action, so crawlers and ai agents that don't run javascript still see everything. there's also an llms.txt, so even the robots get a tour.
  • staying awake: another github action pings supabase every 5 days so the database doesn't doze off.

the telegram bot that runs my site

the worker also doubles as a telegram bot that only i control. every contact message, guestbook entry, reply and reaction lands in my chat, so the site basically texts me when someone shows up.

it also takes commands:

  • /ping checks the whole infrastructure: the worker, the site, supabase, and the cdns i depend on, with latency for each
  • /stats shows today's visits, guestbook entries, reactions, and my current status
  • /status <message> changes the "ovi says" banner on the homepage. i can update my own website from a chat app, in bed, like a professional
  • /about and /help explain what it does

/status is locked to my chat id. anyone else who tries gets a polite "unauthorized".

reactions, guestbook entries, replies, and /stats on demand.

the parts that fought back

  • link previews: browsers can't read other sites' open graph tags (cors), so the worker fetches them. that meant writing an ssrf guard that re-checks every redirect hop. nobody warns you that a chat room can quietly become a "fetch any url for me" machine.
  • impersonation: the second you add a public chat, someone tries to be "admin". reserved names are blocked for everyone except me with a real session token, and bot and ai are blocked even for me, since their replies are written server-side.

the honest part

this was supposed to be a weekend project. it was not a weekend project.

i kept redesigning it. i'd get the look to a place i liked, open it the next day, hate it, and start over. the color direction changed more times than i want to admit. somewhere in there i also decided a static site wasn't enough, so i bolted on a cloudflare worker and supabase, and then spent way too long on stuff the visitor will never see.

the worst part is that i'd already burned out on programming once, and this almost did it again. what fixed it was admitting it's a hobby. no deadline, no audience, nobody to impress. once i stopped treating it like a deliverable, it got fun again, and the site got better too.

what i learned

if your portfolio could belong to anyone, it doesn't really belong to you. put the weird stuff in. keep the sarcasm. make something you'd actually want to open on a random tuesday.

go look at it

repo: https://github.com/iamovi/iamovi.github.io
