it's cc by 4.0, so take it, change it, build on it, just give me credit. even sarcastic people like credit.

articles.title: Converting Centimeters to Inches Without Pretending Rounded Results Are Exact
articles.description: One inch is exactly 2.54 centimeters, but that does not make every centimeter-to-inch result an exact...
articles.body_html:
One inch is exactly 2.54 centimeters, but that does not make every centimeter-to-inch result an exact decimal. I wanted a small conversion page to make that distinction clear: an exact unit definition, a floating-point calculation, and a rounded display are three different things.

This matters when you build a measurement UI. The usual multiplication or division is easy; deciding how many digits to show, what a reverse conversion means, and whether a tiny measurement should disappear is where the numerical contract actually takes shape.

Use Exact Definitions Without Duplicating Pair Formulas

The conversion page uses the same helper as the site's general length converter. Instead of storing a formula for each direction, the helper gives each supported unit a scale relative to meters.

The relevant entries are cm: 0.01 and inch: 0.0254. The actual conversion function is:

export function convertLength(value, fromKey, toKey) {
  const meters = (Number(value) || 0) * (lengthUnitMap[fromKey] || 0);
  return lengthUnitMap[toKey] ? meters / lengthUnitMap[toKey] : 0;
}

For centimeters to inches, it multiplies the input by 0.01 and divides by 0.0254. Algebraically, that is the familiar division by 2.54.

The useful design decision is not making the arithmetic shorter. It is having one unit table serve both the general converter and the fixed-pair page. Correcting a scale or adding a supported unit should not require hunting through many slightly different copies of the same formula.

The inch definition itself is exact. A rounded reciprocal such as 0.3937 inches per centimeter is an approximation, so repeatedly using that shortened multiplier introduces an avoidable source of error before display rounding even begins.

The helper does not use a decimal-arithmetic library, however. Its constants and operations are JavaScript Number values, so the exact definition is still evaluated through binary floating-point arithmetic.

An Exact Constant Does Not Mean an Exact Binary Fraction

Most decimal fractions do not have a finite representation in binary. The same issue that makes 0.1 + 0.2 surprising also applies to ordinary measurement constants.

That does not make JavaScript unusable for a household measurement converter. It means the presentation should not confuse a long sequence of digits with certainty, or assume two algebraically equivalent expressions must produce bit-for-bit identical intermediate results.

The shared helper rounds its output as follows:

export function roundLengthResult(v) {
  if (!isFinite(v)) return 0;
  return Math.round(v * 1e6) / 1e6;
}

For 100 centimeters, the displayed result is 39.370079 inches. For 2.54 centimeters, it is 1 inch. Those are sensible outputs for the page's six-decimal policy.

Notice what the function returns: a number, not a string padded to six decimal places. A result of 1 is displayed as 1, not necessarily 1.000000. “At most six decimal places” is a different promise from “always show six places.”

The limit also concerns decimal places, not significant figures. A value close to zero can lose a much larger proportion of its information than a large value. A single display policy is convenient, but it is not a complete scientific measurement policy.

I would keep input precision, calculation precision, and display precision separate when reviewing a numeric interface. A precise-looking display cannot recover uncertainty in a ruler reading, and rounding output should not be described as increasing the accuracy of the original measurement.

Round Trips Can Lose Information

The fixed-pair page lets the user edit either side. Its left-to-right synchronization writes a rounded output:

toValue.value = categoryConfig.value.round(
  categoryConfig.value.convert(fromValue.value, pair.value.from, pair.value.to),
);

The reverse direction uses the corresponding reverse conversion. A synchronization guard prevents the programmatically written output from immediately rewriting the original input.

That protects the current editing direction, but it does not make rounding invertible. If the user later edits or copies the rounded inch result, that rounded number becomes the next input. Information discarded from the earlier result is no longer available.

A particularly clear boundary is 0.000001 centimeters. Converted to inches, it is about 0.0000003937 before display rounding. The six-decimal helper returns zero. Converting that zero back produces zero centimeters, not the original tiny measurement.

This is quantization, not evidence that the unit factor is wrong. Many different small inputs map to the same displayed number, so no reverse operation can identify which original value produced it.

For tests, I would check representative values with an explicitly chosen tolerance rather than asserting exact equality for every arbitrary round trip. I would also include a tiny input that intentionally rounds to zero. That test documents the actual output contract instead of treating the loss as an unexpected accident.

For ordinary nonnegative values, I can estimate that tolerance from the two rounding steps. Rounding inches to six decimal places contributes at most 0.0000005 inch, or 0.00000127 centimeters. Rounding the reverse result adds at most 0.0000005 centimeters, giving a combined absolute error budget of 0.00000177 centimeters, before allowing for floating-point error. That is a display-rounding budget, not a guarantee about the original measurement's accuracy or extreme numeric inputs.

Unit Conversion Does Not Interpret the Measurement

The page's English content discusses heights and screen sizes. The underlying function only converts a scalar length; it does not know what was measured.

A screen measurement in inches generally describes the diagonal. Converting that diagonal to centimeters does not tell you the display's width or height without an aspect ratio. Similarly, a number of inches is not automatically a feet-and-inches height string.

The rounding helper returns zero when its incoming, unrounded result is nonfinite. That check happens before multiplication by one million: a sufficiently large finite result can still overflow during rounding and return Infinity. For example, converting 1e308 centimeters produces a finite intermediate result, but rounding it overflows. The function does not recheck after scaling.

Input handling is a separate boundary. Both fields use type="number", v-model.number, and min="0". On blur, validateInput checks whether the value converts to a finite, nonnegative number and resets an invalid field to zero. That validation does not run before every conversion. The conversion helper itself also coerces nonnumeric input to zero, so these fallbacks do not establish that every displayed zero represents a genuine zero-length measurement.

For ordinary sizing comparisons, the implementation is useful precisely because its scope is small. For engineering tolerances, explicit error states, locale-aware parsing, or preservation of significant figures, I would define a stricter numeric model rather than silently extending the meaning of this one.

I turned this conversion and its shared rounding policy into a small free tool: CM to Inches Converter.

articles.title: Headless Chrome is a process, not a function: lifecycle, memory and failure modes in browser automation
articles.description: Thirty-seven orphaned browsers and a full /tmp taught me that headless Chrome is a process tree, not a function call: launch and context and page costs, teardown that survives a SIGKILL, why networkidle never fires, readiness as a DOM predicate, locators vs element handles after a re-render, frames and shadow roots, dialogs and downloads, traces for postmortems, and the retries that duplicate a submit.
articles.body_html:
The run died at minute forty with ENOMEM. The task it had been doing was unremarkable — open a page, read a table, fill a form, close. What was remarkable was ps:

$ ps -eo pid,ppid,rss,etime,comm | grep -c headless_shell
37
$ du -sh /tmp/.org.chromium.Chromium.* | tail -3
612M

Thirty-seven browsers, none of them mine anymore, and four hundred gigabytes of profile directories spread across a disk that had sixty. Somewhere in my agent loop, a finally that was supposed to close a browser had been skipped by a task-level timeout, the parent dove off, and the children kept running with nobody to reap them. The next run launched more. The failure looked like a memory bug in my code. It was a process-lifecycle bug in my environment.

That is what this post is about. Not "how to automate a browser" — there are ten thousand tutorials for page.click. This is about the engineering that decides whether a browser automation loop survives a week in production: what the browser's object model actually costs, where the leaks are, why your navigations never "finish", what a selector really guarantees after a re-render, what a trace file buys you at 3 a.m., and which failures you are allowed to retry and which ones will double-charge someone.

Everything below is from an assistant that operates a browser on someone's behalf: filling forms, submitting paperwork, reading account pages, cancelling things. It runs in containers, it is limited to a few hundred megabytes of RAM per worker, and it fails in public.

Three objects, three different costs

Headless Chrome is usually introduced as a function you call. It is a process tree with a handle, and Playwright's object model mirrors that tree. Get the costs right and the rest of the design follows.

Object What it is Rough cost What it owns
Browser one OS process tree, one Chromium build, one launch hundreds of milliseconds, tens of MB idle the event loop, the profile directory, all renderers
BrowserContext an incognito-like profile inside that browser milliseconds cookies, storage, cache, permissions, proxies, storage_state
Page one renderer + a main frame milliseconds to create, tens of MB to hold a document, timers, a network client, its own heap

Two consequences are easy to miss:

Launching a browser per task is the expensive way to get isolation, and the cheap way to run out of processes. Contexts give you cookie isolation, storage isolation, permission isolation and a separate storage_state for essentially nothing. What a context does not give you is process isolation: a renderer crash takes its page with it, and a pathological page can starve its siblings. So the usual shape is one browser per worker, one context per task, one page per document the task actually needs — and a fresh browser every N tasks to shed accumulated renderer baggage.

The context is your security boundary, so make it one. If your assistant ever acts for two different people, or for one person against two different services, the identity lives in the context. Cookies do not leak upward from a context to a browser — they leak across pages inside one context. Any design that reuses a single context "to save time" is a design where a stale session from task A is the session task B acts with. storage_state is a credential file; treat it exactly like the password it stands for.

The lifecycle must not depend on your code finishing

Here is the shape I use in Python. It is longer than async with async_playwright(), and every extra line is a failure I have already had.

import asyncio, os, signal, shutil, tempfile
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright

@asynccontextmanager
async def browser_session():
    profile = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="pw-profile-")
    pw = await async_playwright().start()
    browser = None
    try:
        browser = await pw.chromium.launch(
            headless=True,
            args=[
                "--disable-dev-shm-usage",     # /dev/shm is 64MB in most containers
                "--disable-gpu",
                "--no-first-run",
                "--no-default-browser-check",
                f"--user-data-dir={profile}",
            ],
        )
        yield browser
    finally:
        if browser is not None:
            try:
                await asyncio.wait_for(browser.close(), timeout=10)
            except Exception:
                pass
        await pw.stop()
        shutil.rmtree(profile, ignore_errors=True)

Two notes on that, because both are load-bearing.

The browser.close() is wrapped in a timeout because close can hang. A page in a beforeunload loop, a renderer that has stopped answering, a debugging socket that will not drain: any of them can make a graceful close wait forever. A close that never returns is worse than a kill, because it holds the finally block open and every resource behind it.

The second note is the one that actually fixes the orphans, and it is outside this function. Playwright launches Chromium as a child of its driver process, and the renderer, GPU and utility processes are children of that. If your Python process is killed by a task-level timeout — the supervisor's SIGKILL, not yours — none of your finally blocks run at all, and the whole tree is orphaned. So the real fix has two layers: your code cleans up on its own deadline, and whatever supervises your code must kill a process group, not a process. Start each task with start_new_session=True (Python's subprocess) or in its own container, and kill the group on timeout.

When you need the browser in a group you control explicitly — the case I ended up in — launch Chromium yourself and attach to it. This is public API and it gives you the PID:

proc = subprocess.Popen(
    ["/usr/bin/chromium", "--headless=new", "--remote-debugging-port=0",
     f"--user-data-dir={profile}", "--disable-dev-shm-usage"],
    start_new_session=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
)
endpoint = read_ws_endpoint(proc)          # parse "DevTools listening on ws://..."
browser = await pw.chromium.connect_over_cdp(endpoint)
...
os.killpg(os.getpgid(proc.pid), signal.SIGKILL)   # reaps the entire tree

connect_over_cdp is Chromium-only, and it means Playwright does not own the launch flags or the browser version — a trade worth making exactly when lifecycle control is your problem. Either way, the difference between "one run leaked" and "the host is out of file descriptors by Tuesday" is whether the thing that kills your process knows about its children.

Also worth stating plainly: --no-sandbox is what you need when Chromium runs as root inside a container, and it is a real reduction in isolation. If you can run the browser as a non-root user, do; if you cannot, understand that the flag is why a compromised renderer is a compromised container. --single-process looks like a memory saving and is not: it collapses the site-isolation boundary and turns "a tab crashed" into "the browser did".

And clean the profile directories. They are 20–60 MB each and they are created under /tmp, which on many images is memory-backed. That is the second half of my ENOMEM: not RAM the pages used, but RAM the temporary profiles occupied and never gave back.

A page that never loads, and why "networkidle" is a trap

waitUntil looks like a knob and is actually a question about the document, not about the network:

  • commit — the response has started arriving. The document exists; almost nothing in it does.
  • domcontentloaded — the HTML is parsed. Scripts that run on parse have run. Subresources may still be in flight.
  • load — window.onload fired: images, stylesheets, iframes loaded. This is the default, and on a heavy page it can be the slowest of the four.
  • networkidle — no network connections for 500 ms. Playwright's own documentation discourages it, and the reason is not style.

networkidle is a guess about a network you do not control. A page with a 30-second heartbeat (setInterval(fetch, 30000)), a websocket, a long-polling support widget, or a "someone is viewing this" beacon will never be idle — so your navigation hangs until the timeout and fails a page that was usable twelve seconds ago. The opposite also happens: a page that is idle for 500 ms while a client-side router then fetches the actual content, so "idle" is reached before the data is.

The reliable pattern is: commit or domcontentloaded, then an explicit readiness condition on the DOM, plus a wall clock. And cut the network you do not need, which both speeds the load and makes "quiet" meaningful:

BLOCK = ("image", "media", "font")

async def quiet_network(context):
    async def handler(route, request):
        if request.resource_type in BLOCK and "/api/" not in request.url:
            await route.abort()
        else:
            await route.continue_()
    await context.route("**/*", handler)

Keep that list conservative. Aborting script or stylesheet changes what the page is — lazy content often loads via script, and a layout that depends on a font metric can move the button you were about to click. Aborting image is usually safe for reading a table; aborting it on a page whose print layout you need is not.

Readiness is a predicate, not an event

The most useful function in my stack is about thirty lines and has saved me more debugging than any other:

async def stable(page, selector: str, quiet_ms: int = 700, timeout_ms: int = 15000):
    """Return when the element's inner HTML has not changed for quiet_ms."""
    last, since = None, None
    deadline = asyncio.get_event_loop().time() + timeout_ms / 1000
    while asyncio.get_event_loop().time() < deadline:
        try:
            html = await page.locator(selector).first.inner_html(timeout=2000)
        except Exception:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
            continue
        now = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()
        if html != last:
            last, since = html, now
        elif now - since >= quiet_ms / 1000:
            return html
        await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    raise TimeoutError(f"{selector} never settled")

Why stability rather than presence: a table that has rendered its header and one row passes any "element exists" check, and then you read nine rows instead of two hundred. A list that is being sorted passes it twice. Requiring the same HTML across a window catches the difference between "rendered" and "finished rendering", which is the failure that produces plausible wrong data rather than an error.

Add one more guard for pages that are never quiet: anchor on a completion signal the site itself provides — a row count matching a total in the page, a "no more results" node, a status column that left a pending state. If the site gives you no such signal, that is a fact worth writing down, because the alternative is a timeout that looks like a bug forever.

Selectors: what a locator promises, and what it does not

A Locator is a query, not a handle. It re-resolves on every action, which is why it survives re-renders — and why the same selector can act on a different element two seconds later. That property is the whole design, and it forces a rule:

Never hold a reference across an await, and always scope the query to the record you mean.

Auto-waiting does more than retry. Before acting, Playwright waits for the element to be attached, visible, stable (not animating), enabled, editable where relevant, and to actually receive the event — meaning it is not covered by an overlay. That last check is what saves you from clicking a cookie banner's twin. When it fails, it says so; treat the message as information, not noise:

element is not visible
element is outside of the viewport
element is not stable
element intercepts pointer events
strict mode violation: locator resolved to 2 elements

Ranking of selector strategies by how long they last, from my own churn:

  1. Role + accessible name (get_by_role("button", name="Cancel")) — survives CSS refactors and layout rewrites, because if the name changes the site broke for screen readers too.
  2. Label / placeholder for form fields (get_by_label("Card number")) — same reason.
  3. A test id (get_by_test_id), when the site has them, because they are there on purpose.
  4. Structural CSS (div:nth-child(3) > span), which is a promise the site never made.
  5. Text — excellent for a button whose text is the meaning, terrible for a cell whose text is data.

The trap is not picking the "wrong" strategy. It is picking a strategy that matches two things, because then the same code either throws (strict mode violation) or, with .first, silently acts on the wrong one. Two "Cancel" buttons on one page is not an edge case; it is what every list view looks like. Scope it:

row = page.get_by_role("row").filter(
    has=page.get_by_role("cell", name="ORD-4417")
)
await row.get_by_role("button", name="Cancel").click()

And when you cannot express "the row for this order" as a locator, stop and reconsider the step. An automation that cannot name its target per-record is an automation that will eventually cancel someone else's booking.

Detachment is not an exception to catch. It is a signal about your code.

Sooner or later everything throws one of these:

Element is not attached to the DOM
Execution context was destroyed, most likely because of a navigation
Target page, context or browser has been closed

The first two mean the node you resolved is gone, because the framework re-rendered the subtree, a virtual list recycled the row, or the document navigated. There is exactly one correct response: re-resolve the locator and act again, from a fresh read of the page. Not "retry the click with the old handle" — that is the same stale node. And not "catch and continue", because the action did not happen.

# WRONG: the handle is a snapshot of one moment
handle = await page.query_selector("text=Submit")
await page.wait_for_timeout(300)
await handle.click()          # Element is not attached to the DOM

# RIGHT: the locator re-resolves each time it is used
await page.wait_for_timeout(300)
await page.get_by_role("button", name="Submit").click()

Execution context was destroyed is the same fact at the document level: a navigation happened somewhere between your two calls, including a same-origin <form> submit you triggered. If it appears after a click, do not retry the click — check whether the click actually worked. This is the cheap version of a much larger problem: retrying an action whose effect you have not established is how a submit becomes two submissions.

Frames, shadow roots, and the places a document hides

An iframe is a document with its own origin, its own JS context, and — commonly — the thing that holds your control. A payment widget, a captcha, a date picker, an embedded form. Playwright's frame_locator waits for the frame to appear and scopes everything after it:

frame = page.frame_locator("iframe[title='Payment']")
await frame.get_by_label("Card number").fill(card_number)

Three things people get wrong:

  • Matching the iframe by URL. Frame URLs change per session (tokens, tenant ids). Match by title, name, or position scoped under a container — and if there is exactly one frame, say so explicitly rather than using the first one you find.
  • Nested frames. A card form inside a 3-D Secure flow inside the payment iframe is three documents. frame_locator composes, but your readiness predicate must run inside the innermost one.
  • Shadow DOM. Playwright's CSS engine pierces open shadow roots, so a get_by_role inside a web component usually works. A closed shadow root is genuinely unreachable from script, by design. When a control is invisible for that reason, the order form is telling you it wants a human, and that is a handover, not a puzzle to solve.

The hard line I keep in code and in the docs of my own tool: no stealth patches, no user-agent or canvas or WebGL spoofing, no CAPTCHA solving, no "human typing" emulation. Every one of those is a decision about someone else's system made without their consent, and they also fail quietly in ways that cost more than they save: a solver that half-works turns a clear "stop and ask the user" into a corrupted submission. When the browser hits a bot check, a one-time code, a passkey prompt, or a 3-D Secure step, the correct action is to stop, persist the page state, and hand back an action a person can finish in ten seconds.

Dialogs, downloads, uploads, popups

These are the four places where a click does something outside the document, and each has a one-line mistake that costs an hour.

Dialogs. If no listener is attached, Playwright auto-dismisses alert, confirm and prompt. So a confirm("Delete this record?") returns false and the delete silently does not happen — you will swear the click worked, because it did. Register the handler before the click, and log every dialog with its message, because the message is the only place the page tells you what it just asked:

page.on("dialog", lambda d: (print("DIALOG:", d.type, d.message), asyncio.create_task(d.accept())))

Downloads. A click that starts a download produces no navigation and no DOM change, so an agent that waits for a page transition waits forever. Wrap the click:

async with page.expect_download() as info:
    await page.get_by_role("button", name="Download invoice").click()
download = await info.value
await download.save_as("/data/out/invoice.pdf")
print(download.suggested_filename, await download.path())

Beware the variant that opens a PDF in a viewer tab instead of downloading: expect_popup then, and a PDF viewer is a plugin document with no useful DOM. If you need the bytes, take them from response.body() on the request that produced the document.

Uploads. set_input_files on the input[type=file] is reliable; clicking a "Choose file" button and driving an OS file picker is not available in headless mode at all. If the site hides the input, set_input_files still works on a hidden input — that is not a bypass, it is the normal path.

Popups. expect_popup and then work in the new page, remembering that the opener's context is what holds the cookies. Close popups you do not need; each is a renderer.

Record what the page said, or debug by guesswork

The single highest-value thing I added after the orphans incident is a ring buffer of the browser's own complaints, dumped into the failure record:

class PageLog:
    def __init__(self, page, limit=200):
        self.events, self.limit = [], limit
        page.on("console", lambda m: self.add("console", m.type, m.text))
        page.on("pageerror", lambda e: self.add("pageerror", str(e)))
        page.on("requestfailed", lambda r: self.add("requestfailed", r.url, r.failure))
        page.on("response", lambda r: r.status >= 400 and self.add("http", r.status, r.url))
        page.on("crash", lambda p: self.add("crash", "page crashed"))

    def add(self, *parts):
        self.events.append(" ".join(str(p) for p in parts)[:400])
        del self.events[:-self.limit]

Two rules make it useful. Capture console messages of type error and warning only at first — a modern app logs hundreds of lines and the signal drowns. And capture response status ≥ 400, because the most common silent failure in browser automation is not a broken selector: it is a 401 or a 422 on the XHR your click triggered, in a page that rendered an optimistic UI and moved on.

Traces, HAR, and the artifact that answers "what did it see?"

When a run fails in a container at 3 a.m., the only question that matters is what the page looked like at the moment of failure. Console logs do not answer it. A trace does.

await context.tracing.start(screenshots=True, snapshots=True, sources=True)
try:
    ...task...
finally:
    path = f"/data/traces/{task_id}.zip"
    await context.tracing.stop(path=path)

A trace is a timeline of DOM snapshots, screenshots, network, console and source, openable in a viewer, and it is the difference between "the button was not there" and "the button was there, disabled, behind a modal with a 3-second fade". It is also large — hundreds of kilobytes to tens of megabytes. So: trace the failure, not the run. Start tracing always, discard on success (stop() without a path), keep on failure. If your Playwright version supports chunking, keep the last few chunks instead of one long recording.

HAR is the complement for network shape: record_har_path with record_har_content="omit" gives you every request, status, timing and size in a portable file, without the bodies that make a HAR unusable (and without the customer data that makes it a liability). "embed" is for the case where a body is the evidence — and then it is a document you must store like one.

Screenshots are the last resort, and they have a specific use: the picture the user needs when you ask them to take over. A full-page screenshot at the moment of handover plus one sentence of what is needed beats any JSON.

Retry semantics: three classes, one table

Retries are where browser automation turns a flaky test into a duplicate charge. The classification I use is by observable state, not by exception type:

Class Examples Retry?
Never started navigation refused, net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET before any response, browser has been closed before the click Yes, with backoff
Read-only reading a table, listing rows, checking a status page Yes, freely — no side effect to duplicate
Started, outcome unknown click on a submit, then timeout or context destroyed No. Read the record first

The third class is the one that matters. "Started, unknown" is not a retry problem, it is a read problem: navigate to the record list, find the row you were creating, and act on what is there. If the product gives you no way to read what happened, then the correct behaviour is to stop and report — a duplicate order you caused is worse than an order you did not place.

Two implementation notes that keep retries honest:

  • Retry from a known state. A retry that resumes mid-flow reuses a page whose state you no longer trust. Go back to the URL you started from and run the step again, so the retry is the same experiment.
  • Cap and count. Bounded attempts, exponential backoff with full jitter, and two metrics: retries and retries_exhausted. Retries above a couple of percent of tasks is a design smell — usually a readiness predicate that is wrong, or a selector that matches the wrong row.

Memory, concurrency, and the number that decides your worker size

Browser automation looks I/O-bound and is partly CPU-bound: each renderer parses, styles and lays out its own document, and a busy page can hold a core. So parallelism past your core count helps only for the parts that are waiting.

The memory question has an empirical answer, and you should measure it rather than trust anyone's table:

# RSS of everything under one worker, sampled while it works
watch -n2 'ps -eo rss,comm | grep -E "headless_shell|chrome" | awk "{s+=\$1} END {print s/1024 \" MB\"}"'

What I do with the number: pick a per-page ceiling from measurement (a light page and a heavy app differ by a lot, so measure your heaviest), leave 30–40% of the container above the sum of your concurrency, and enforce it with a semaphore rather than by trusting the scheduler.

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(4)          # = allowed concurrent pages

async def run_task(task):
    async with sem:
        async with browser_session() as browser:
            ctx = await browser.new_context(accept_downloads=True)
            try:
                await do(task, ctx)
            finally:
                await ctx.close()

And recycle: a long-lived browser accumulates dead renderers, cached compiled code and fragmented heaps. Restart it every N tasks or after a memory threshold, whichever comes first. Restarting a browser is a second; restarting a container because the OOM killer chose your process is a page.

Boundaries, permissions, and the parts that are not engineering

Headless Chrome will do what you tell it, which is the problem. Four rules I would put in any automation that acts for someone:

One identity per context, and none of them borrowed. No shared storage_state across tasks, no "just use my cookies", no acting for person B with person A's session. The context is the identity; a leak here is a data leak, not a bug.

Rate and volume limits are part of design, not politeness. A loop that pages through a site's search results is a scraper. Enforce a per-host concurrency of one or two, sleep between pages, respect robots.txt and the site's terms, and never let a retry loop turn into a traffic spike — a hundred retries per minute is what a macro looks like to the site, and being blocked is the gentle outcome.

Log every navigation with what it was for. A URL list with timestamps, task ids and purposes is the only way to answer "did it go where I said it would" after the fact, including for the pages it visited on its own.

Decide the irreversible ones in advance. Which clicks in your flow cannot be undone, what the amount is before it goes out, and whether the person agreed to it. An assistant that discovers the total at the confirmation step and proceeds anyway has made a decision that was never its own. The engineering version of that rule: never retry the irreversible step without reading state first, and never let a timeout on it be treated as a failure.

What headless cannot do

Being honest about this saves weeks:

  • It is not the browser your user has. Chromium builds used by automation commonly lack proprietary media codecs, so an H.264 player renders a black box. Canvas and WebGL rendering, font hinting and PDF output differ from Chrome and Safari in ways that matter if the task is "does this look right".
  • Some sites refuse it by design. That is their call. Spoofing past it is not a workaround, it is a violation; change the route (an official API, a partner endpoint, a person) instead.
  • PDF rendering is a separate engine. If the output of the task is a PDF, print it, keep it, and read the file — because the page being "visible" says nothing about what landed in the document.
  • When you genuinely need a real browser, attach over CDP to a browser a person launched (connect_over_cdp) or run headed inside a virtual display. Same API, different trust and resource story — and the right answer when the site's own bot defences are checking for things that only a real session has.

Fixtures: make the failure modes run in CI

Every behaviour above has a small, deterministic reproduction, and I keep them as files that a test can open from file://. Not because they are hard, but because the tests are what stop the finally from being deleted by a future refactor.

Fixture What it does What the test asserts
detach.html re-renders a list every 200 ms a held ElementHandle click fails with "not attached"; a Locator click succeeds
dialog.html confirm() on submit with no handler the submit is a no-op; with a handler it fires once
poller.html setInterval(fetch, 30000) waitUntil="networkidle" times out; domcontentloaded + readiness succeeds
frames.html control inside a nested iframe frame_locator path works; top-level selector does not
slow.html renders 1 row then 200 after 3 s presence-check reads 1 row; stability reads 200
oversize.html 20 MB of inline images with image aborted, memory and time drop measurably

The one that pays for itself is detach.html. It is the fixture that keeps a team from "fixing" a flake by adding a sleep(1000).

Checklist

The list I actually keep, in order of how much each item has cost me when missing:

  • Every launch is paired with a guaranteed teardown, and the supervision layer kills a process group, not a process.
  • close() has its own timeout, and a hung close is killed rather than waited on.
  • Profile directories are created per launch, on a real filesystem, and deleted.
  • --disable-dev-shm-usage is set wherever /dev/shm is small.
  • The container's memory is sized from measured per-page RSS plus headroom, not from a blog's table.
  • Concurrency is enforced by a semaphore, and the browser is recycled every N tasks.
  • Navigation uses commit/domcontentloaded plus an explicit readiness predicate; networkidle is not used.
  • Readiness is stability over a window or the site's own completion signal, with a wall-clock cap.
  • Unneeded resource types are blocked conservatively — never document or script.
  • Selectors are role/label based, scoped to the record, and never .first on a query that can match siblings.
  • No element handle is held across an await; detachment is recovered by re-resolving, never by retrying the old handle.
  • Frames are matched by title/name/structure, not by URL; nested frames are handled explicitly.
  • A dialog handler is registered before the first click that might raise one, and every dialog is logged.
  • Downloads use expect_download and an explicit save path; uploads use set_input_files.
  • Console errors, page errors, failed requests and HTTP ≥ 400 responses are captured and attached to failures.
  • A trace is kept for failures and discarded on success; HAR content is omitted unless a body is the evidence.
  • Retries are classified: never-started and read-only retry with backoff; started-and-unknown never retries without reading state.
  • Bot checks, one-time codes, passkeys and payment authentication stop the task and hand it to a person, with the page left where it was.

None of this is exotic. It is what happens when you take seriously that the thing you are driving is not a function that returns a page — it is a process tree with a heap, a network, and no obligation to tell you the truth about whether it finished. The finally you forgot is still running on someone's machine.

Disclosure: I build small automation tools and write about the parts that break. I also maintain an English guide for an AI assistant app whose invite system I use as a concrete example of these ideas: Pickle invite code — what the app does and how to enter it and the invite link pickle.com/i/RDKXK77G9ZRT. If someone joins through that link I receive in-app usage credit; it costs the person joining nothing. Nothing in this article depends on that product, and every pattern above is generic.

articles.title: An offline write queue for React Native, and the two reader questions that changed it
articles.description: Short answer: Bareship queues offline writes with TanStack Query: a paused mutation is saved to MMKV,...
articles.body_html:
Short answer: Bareship queues offline writes with TanStack Query: a paused mutation is saved to MMKV, so it survives the app being killed, and replays in order when the phone reconnects. Every write gets an Idempotency-Key when the user taps, reused for every attempt, so the server applies it once. Since 0.4.0, each write also records the account that made it and is never sent for anyone else, and a write can cancel the dependent writes queued behind it if the server rejects it.

In the launch post I said Bareship saves a like made offline, keeps it through a
restart and sends it once when the phone reconnects, and promised the next post would show how.

Two readers on dev.to then asked questions I hadn't fully answered. Dave Kurian
asked whose write it is when someone else signs in before it's sent. Odd Eggs Studio
asked what happens to the writes behind one the server rejects. Both answers are now code, released in
0.4.0. This post walks through the queue from the tap
to the server, with those two changes in the places they belong.

What can go wrong with one like

Someone likes a post on a train with no signal. Before that like reaches your server, any of these can happen:

  1. The user swipes the app away, or the OS kills it.
  2. The request goes out, the connection drops before the answer comes back, and the app tries again. Now the server has seen it twice.
  3. They like, then unlike. The two requests arrive in the wrong order.
  4. They sign out and someone else signs in on the same phone. The like is still waiting.
  5. The server refuses the like for good, and three edits that depend on it are queued behind it.

A queue that only handles the first one still looks fine in a demo. The other four show up later, in bug reports
you can't reproduce. (For the wider design questions, such as a local database, conflicts and photo uploads, see my
offline-first data layer post. This one is about the write queue
only.)

The base: TanStack Query, with the gaps filled

Bareship doesn't have its own queue engine. TanStack Query already does most of the work:

  • A mutation with networkMode: 'online' pauses while the phone is offline instead of failing, and resumes when the connection returns.
  • Paused mutations can be saved with the query cache. Bareship stores that cache in MMKV, so a waiting write survives the app being killed.
  • Mutations that share a scope run one at a time, in the order they were made. That handles problem 3.

The gap is in what gets saved. A restored mutation is only data: its key and its variables. The functions that
send it and update the screen aren't saved, because you can't save a function. TanStack Query looks them up by
the mutation's key in the defaults registered on the client. If nothing is registered yet when the saved cache
comes back, the write fails with "No mutationFn found".

In React Native that's easy to get wrong. Metro loads modules lazily, so the feature that defines the like may not
have run yet when the cache is restored at startup. Bareship fixes this with one file, src/app/queued-writes.ts,
which imports every module that defines a queued write and is imported before the cache is restored. A test fails
if a definition is missing from it. A write whose definition really is gone, say removed in an app update, is
dropped and logged at startup instead of crashing.

From the feature's side, a queued write is one definition at module level:

src/features/feed/api.ts

const likeKey = ['posts', 'like'] as const;

export const useToggleLike = defineQueuedMutation<Post, { postId: string; like: boolean }>({
  mutationKey: likeKey,
  mutationFn: ({ postId, like, idempotencyKey }) => {
    const url = `/posts/${encodeURIComponent(postId)}/like`;
    return like
      ? http.post(url, PostSchema, { idempotencyKey })
      : http.delete(url, PostSchema, { idempotencyKey });
  },
  onMutate: async ({ postId, like }) => {
    await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: postKeys.all });
    updatePost(queryClient, postId, applyLike(like)); // show it at once
  },
  onError: (_error, { postId, like }) => {
    updatePost(queryClient, postId, applyLike(!like)); // undo it
    toast.error(i18n.t('feed.likeFailed'));
  },
  onSuccess: (updated, { postId }) => {
    // A like then an unlike queued offline: keep the optimistic state until the last one lands.
    if (hasLaterWrite(likeKey, variables => variables.postId === postId)) return;
    updatePost(queryClient, updated.id, () => updated);
  },
});

The cache work lives in these callbacks, not in the screen, because after a restart the screen that started the
write is gone. The variables are saved as JSON, so they stay small: ids and flags, not whole objects.

The "Waiting to sync" label comes from the paused writes themselves. useWaitingWrites(likeKey) returns the
variables of every like still waiting, and the banner under the header counts them. Nothing is tracked twice.

Sent twice, applied once: idempotency keys

Problem 2 can't be solved on the phone alone. If the connection drops after the server got the request, the app
can't know whether the like landed. It has to try again, so the server has to recognise a repeat.

Every queued write gets an Idempotency-Key (a random UUID) when the user taps, not when the request is sent.
That one key goes with every attempt:

  • The HTTP client retries network errors, timeouts, 408, 429 and 5xx with backoff, up to 3 attempts in all. It reuses the key each time.
  • A write replayed after a restart reuses the key.
  • A write the server already answered is never sent again.

On the server, the rule is to store the first response for each key and return it for repeats. Here's the mock
backend that ships with the template, which does exactly that for likes:

src/mocks/handlers.ts

const key = request.headers.get('Idempotency-Key');
const replay = key ? db.idempotency.get(key) : undefined;
if (replay) return HttpResponse.json(replay); // seen it: same answer, applied once

// ...apply the like...
const body = postDto(post, user.id);
if (key) db.idempotency.set(key, body);
return HttpResponse.json(body);

One limit, written down in the code: a write that's already on the wire when the app dies isn't saved, because
it's no longer paused. Its key still makes a manual retry safe.

Question 1: whose write is it?

Dave's question was about problem 4. A like is queued, the user signs out, someone else signs in, the phone
reconnects. Does the first user's like go out with the second user's token?

My answer at the time was "no, because sign-out clears the queue". That was true, but the guarantee lived in the
sign-out flow. Any future change there, like account switching or a sign-out that fails halfway, could break it
without anyone noticing. Dave suggested storing the account next to the key, and he was right.

Now each write records who made it:

src/data/offline.ts

mutate: variables =>
  mutation.mutate({ ...variables, idempotencyKey: createId(), accountId: currentAccount() }),

It's checked twice. The first check is when the saved queue comes back after a restart. The second is just before
each write is sent, because the account can change while a write waits offline:

src/data/offline.ts

mutationFn: variables => {
  if (!belongsToCurrentAccount(variables)) throw new OtherAccountWriteError();
  return mutationFn(variables);
},

A write from another account is dropped and logged. It never reaches the server, and it doesn't call the
feature's onError, so the new user doesn't see someone else's rollback or error message. Writes saved by older
versions have no account id and replay as before.

The server side matters too: keep idempotency keys per user, so a replayed key can never match another account's
record. That's now in the docs.

Question 2: what if the server says no?

Odd Eggs Studio asked about problem 5. If a queued write is rejected, does the queue stop or carry on?

It carries on, and for likes that's right: each like stands alone, so one refused like shouldn't block the next.
But some writes depend on each other. "Create a draft, then edit it" is the usual example. If the create fails,
sending the edit only produces a second error, and the screen is left showing a draft that doesn't exist.

So defineQueuedMutation now takes onRejected:

src/features/drafts/api.ts

export const useCreateDraft = defineQueuedMutation<Draft, { draftId: string; title: string }>({
  mutationKey: ['drafts', 'create'],
  scope: 'drafts',
  onRejected: 'cancel-scope', // if this fails for good, drop the drafts writes queued behind it
  mutationFn: …,
});

export const useEditDraft = defineQueuedMutation<Draft, { draftId: string; body: string }>({
  mutationKey: ['drafts', 'edit'],
  scope: 'drafts',
  mutationFn: …,
  onError: (error, { draftId }) => {
    // Runs for a cancelled edit too (error.kind === 'cancelled'): undo its optimistic update.
  },
});

The details that took the most thought:

  • "Fails for good" means the server refused the write, or it still failed after the HTTP client's retries. Going offline isn't a failure: the queue just pauses.
  • Each cancelled write gets its own onError, with an error of kind 'cancelled'. Every write rolls back its own optimistic update, so the screen ends up correct without the failed write having to know what came after it.
  • Only writes already queued are cancelled. Something the user does after the failure runs normally.
  • The limit: if the app is killed between the failure and the next launch, the cancellation isn't remembered. The writes behind it go out and fail on their own, as they did before. I wrote this down in the docs instead of adding more machinery for a rare case.

What I took from this

Both changes came from comments on a launch post. Each one turned into an issue, a change with tests, a docs
section and a release. Two things stood out to me:

  • Put a guarantee in the data, not in a flow. "Sign-out clears the queue" was true, but it depended on code far from the queue. "Every write knows its account" stays true whatever happens elsewhere.
  • Default to the simple behaviour, and make the strict one a single line. Most writes are independent, so 'continue' stays the default. The chains that need more get 'cancel-scope', and the limit is written next to it.

Try it 

npx create-bareship Acme
cd Acme
pnpm android   # or: pnpm ios

Sign in with demo@example.com / password123, turn on airplane mode, like a post, close the app, open it again,
then turn airplane mode off. The like is sent once. The mock backend runs inside the app, so you don't need a
server for any of this.

  • Queue code: src/data/offline.ts
  • Guide: Offline and writes that depend on each other
  • The two changes: #28 (account) and #29 (onRejected)

Next in the series: an architecture the linter enforces. Layers and feature boundaries that ESLint checks, so
code review doesn't have to.

If you have a question like Dave's or Odd Eggs Studio's, leave it in the comments on dev.to or open an issue. Two of
them have already made the template better.

FAQ

How does Bareship keep offline writes after the app is killed?

Queued writes are TanStack Query mutations that pause while offline. Paused mutations are saved with the query
cache in MMKV and replayed in order on the next launch, once every write's definition is registered.

How does Bareship stop a write from being applied twice?

Each write gets an Idempotency-Key when the user taps, and every retry or replay sends the same key. The server
stores the first response for each key and returns it for repeats.

Can a queued write be sent under another user's account?

No. Since 0.4.0 each write records the account that made it, and it's checked on restore and before every send.
A write from another account is dropped and logged, without calling the feature's error handler.

Takeaways

  • Bareship's offline queue is TanStack Query paused mutations, saved to MMKV and replayed in order after a restart.
  • Register every queued write's definition before the saved cache is restored: Metro loads modules lazily.
  • One Idempotency-Key per write, made when the user taps and reused for every attempt, so the server applies it once.
  • Each queued write records its account and is checked on restore and before every send (0.4.0).
  • onRejected: 'cancel-scope' drops the dependent writes behind a rejected one, and each rolls back its own update.

articles.title: JavaScript noindex Removal: Fix the Initial HTML Before Trusting the DOM
articles.description: If a public page's initial HTML contains a noindex robots tag, do not rely on JavaScript to remove it...
articles.body_html:
If a public page's initial HTML contains a noindex robots tag, do not rely on JavaScript to remove it later. Fix the initial response for the pages intended to be indexed, then verify the rendered document and the route states separately. A clean browser DOM is useful evidence, but it does not erase an earlier directive in a different processing path.

For a SaaS team, this can hide a clear buyer answer behind a template mistake. The product page may describe a real capability, load normally and pass a visual review. The writer keeps improving the answer while the original response still tells a search engine to exclude it. Trace the directive before expanding the copy.

Establish the intended policy for the exact URL

Start by naming the public page and deciding whether it is supposed to be eligible for indexing. Record the full URL, including any query string relevant to the problem. Do not begin by deleting every noindex tag across the application. A public product explanation and a private account screen have different purposes, even when they share a frontend shell.

Write down the reason for the intended policy. A product guide may answer a buyer question that the company wants people to find. A temporary internal preview may intentionally stay out of search. That distinction belongs in the diagnosis, so a developer does not “repair” a deliberate publishing choice while trying to help marketing.

Keep access protection separate from this editorial policy. Removing an indexing directive is not a reason to publish private content or weaken authentication. Work on a public, approved page and preserve the existing protection around other routes. If the intended audience is unclear, resolve that specific question with the page owner before changing the response.

Inspect the initial HTML before the rendered head

Google's JavaScript SEO documentation warns that encountering noindex may cause Google to skip rendering and JavaScript execution. Removing or changing that tag with JavaScript may therefore fail to have the intended effect. Google advises against putting noindex in the original code when the page should be indexed.

Use that documented behavior to choose the first diagnostic step. Capture the response for the exact public URL using your normal development tools. Search the returned HTML for robots directives and retain the relevant portion of the head. Record the response conditions and release version alongside the finding so another developer can reproduce it.

Then inspect the rendered head in a fresh browser load. Compare what arrived with what the application eventually produced. If the initial response says noindex and the later document does not, that difference is the issue to investigate. Avoid calling the later DOM the “real page” in a way that makes the earlier response disappear from the evidence.

Trace which layer supplied the directive

A fictional product, Fieldglass Notes, uses one application shell for public guides and account pages. Its public guide about approval history receives a default noindex tag. After the page loads, a component removes the tag for public content. This is a hypothetical failure pattern, not an observed behavior of a real service.

The fix begins with ownership. Ask which part of the publishing path creates the initial head: a template, a route-specific server response, a static export or another documented layer in that application. Follow the actual output back to its source. Do not assume the page component that removes the tag also owns the response that added it.

Propose a narrow change: public guide URLs receive their intended initial indexing policy, while account and preview routes keep theirs. Review a representative URL from each affected class. The important regression question is not merely whether one guide lost noindex. It is whether the implementation now applies the right policy to each type of page it serves.

Verify direct loads and client-side navigation

Test a direct request to the repaired URL. Start a new browser context or use the team's established method for checking an uncached public response. Confirm that the initial HTML carries the intended policy, then inspect the resulting rendered head. Save both observations against the same release so the evidence describes one implementation.

Next, navigate to the guide through the application. Check the final URL and head after moving between pages with different policies. A direct load and an in-app transition are separate test cases. This is a recommended regression check for applications with changing route state, not a claim that every framework has the same metadata behavior.

For Fieldglass Notes, use the public guide, a public error route and a protected account route as clearly separate cases. Do not log private account content into a public SEO report. The developer can record whether the expected policy remained in place without copying confidential page text. Keep the test evidence proportional to the actual defect being investigated.

Check error states without turning every failure into an answer

A public page should not become an indexable empty shell merely because the initial tag was removed. Examine what the application displays when its content request fails or the requested item does not exist. Record how those states are intended to behave and compare the response and rendered output with that policy.

Google's JavaScript guide includes approaches to handling client-side error pages. Follow the parts relevant to the site's actual implementation rather than copying an isolated example into every route. In particular, distinguish a real missing resource from a temporary data-fetch problem. The right implementation depends on what the page can truthfully return under those conditions.

The editorial check is straightforward: can a reader reach the promised public answer on a normal load? If the answer disappears after a content request, a correct robots directive alone has not completed the task. Give the content availability problem its own ticket and evidence. Do not hide it under a general label such as “Google has trouble with JavaScript.”

Verify the saved buyer answer after the repair

Return to the passage that made the page worth discovering. For the fictional approval-history guide, that might explain which events are retained and who can view them. Check that the actual public page still contains the answer and its qualifiers. A technical repair should preserve the useful explanation rather than replacing it with a thin diagnostic placeholder.

Use the relevant native inspection tools to examine the repaired public output. Record which view was checked, the URL, the date and the specific directive or passage observed. A successful rendering observation is evidence about that test. It should not be reported as a guarantee of indexing, ranking or a citation in an AI-generated answer.

Keep engine-specific claims bounded. This article's warning about initial noindex comes from Google's documentation. Do not assume Claude, ChatGPT or every other retrieval system processes the same response in the same way. If the business question concerns another surface, use its current guidance and collect observations there as a separate investigation.

Leave a handoff that prevents the same mistake

The completion note should name the original response, the source of its directive and the narrow change made. Include the affected route classes and the cases checked after the repair. “Fixed SEO metadata” hides too much. “Public guide responses no longer inherit the account-shell noindex default” describes a reviewable outcome for this hypothetical application.

Add one meaningful regression check at the layer that introduced the problem. Its purpose is to catch an unintended initial directive on a public route while preserving the intended policy elsewhere. Avoid a large suite of tests that simply repeats the implementation line by line. The useful test fails when the public/private policy boundary is crossed again.

Finally, return the discovery question to the content team with honest limits. The initial HTML and rendered document have been checked for the intended policy; later indexing and AI visibility remain outcomes to observe. That handoff lets writers improve buyer answers for a clear reason, while developers can show that the public delivery path is no longer contradicting the page's purpose.

articles.title: Ma — a rehearsal prompter that waits for you to breathe
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.           What I Built   Ma (間) is a...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.

What I Built

Ma (間) is a small desktop teleprompter for practising a talk, a pitch or an interview answer.

Most rehearsal tools time your words. Ma watches the thing that actually derails a talk: you speed up when your body speeds up. It reads your pulse and breathing from the webcam with the SmartSpectra SDK and uses them in two ways.

  1. While you rehearse. Ma first takes a 30-second calm reference while you sit still. Then you read your script line by line and press Space for the next one. When your pulse climbs 10 bpm or your breathing climbs 5 breaths/min above your own reference, Ma holds the next line and asks for one slow breath. It watches the chest trace and releases the line as soon as it sees that breath (or after 9 seconds, so you are never stuck).
  2. Afterwards. Ma shows the script again with a heat bar on every line for how far your pulse ran above your reference, how much of the line you were talking, your blink rate, and a short list of "plan a pause here" spots for the next run.

"Ma" is the Japanese word for the pause that gives rhythm to speech. The app is built around one idea: the pause is part of the talk, and your body tells you where it belongs.

Demo

Video (1 min 49 s): https://github.com/Class-now/pace-prompter/releases/download/v1.0.0/ma-demo.mp4

The video is a real rehearsal with a live webcam and the live SmartSpectra readings: the opt-in screen, the 30-second calm reference (shown at 5x speed), three breath pauses triggered when breathing ran above my own reference, and the review screen at the end. The face is blurred with Ma's own preview option, and the video has no sound; captions explain each step.

Code

https://github.com/Class-now/pace-prompter

  • Electron app, plain JavaScript, @smartspectra/node-sdk 3.4.0
  • src/core.js holds the pacing logic with no DOM or SDK dependency and is covered by npm test
  • test/sdk-smoke.mjs is a headless check against the real SDK: it pushes a recorded face video through useCustomInput() / sendFrame() and passes when pulse and breathing readings appear
  • Setup: npm install, put SMARTSPECTRA_API_KEY=... in .env, npm start

How It Responds to Human Signals

SmartSpectra signal What Ma does with it
cardio.pulseRate calm reference during calibration; live readout; breath-pause trigger (+10 bpm over your reference); per-line heat in the review
breathing.rate calm reference; breath-pause trigger (+5 breaths/min over your reference)
breathing.upperTrace drawn as the live breath line; detects the one full breath that releases a pause
face.talking shows whether you are speaking; share of each line spent talking
face.blinking blinks per minute per line in the review

Every comparison is against the same person's reading from a minute earlier, never against a population norm. A pulse of 95 means nothing on its own; a pulse that jumped from 72 to 90 in the middle of your second paragraph is exactly what you want to know before you give the talk for real. Ma also reads the SDK's validation status ("Hold still", "Face the camera", "Only one face is allowed") and shows it under the preview, so you can fix your framing before the calm reference is taken.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Opt-in every time. Nothing starts until you tick the consent box on the first screen, which says what is measured and why. The camera light is on only between Start and the review screen.
  • Camera only. Ma never requests the microphone. The app's permission handler refuses every permission except video for its own local page.
  • What leaves the machine. The SmartSpectra SDK reaches Presage's service with your API key to produce measurements. Ma turns the SDK's optional usage telemetry off (enableTelemetry: false). Ma itself has no server and sends nothing anywhere.
  • What is stored. Nothing. Video frames are never written to disk. The numbers for the current run live in memory and are gone when you close the window or start again. The only way a result leaves the app is the Copy report button, which puts a Markdown summary on your clipboard.
  • Who is measured. Only the person who started the session and is sitting in front of the camera. Ma is built for self-rehearsal.
  • No health claims. Readings are shown as pacing notes relative to your own resting reference, never as a judgement about health or emotion. Ma is not a medical device.

Agent Session

I built Ma with Claude Code as a pair: I described the rehearsal problem and the "compare only with yourself" rule, and the agent wrote the pacing logic and tests first, then the Electron shell and SDK wiring. One thing the agent found along the way: on Windows the SDK's useFile() input reports kInputUnavailable, so the headless test pushes frames through useCustomInput() / sendFrame() instead, which is the same path the app uses for the camera.

Web Models API: Practical Guide

In the last article, I focused on why I think an API that exposes open-weight, on-device models to web apps is desperately needed, and why the Web Models API could be a good solution.

In this article, I want to get down to brass tacks and show what the code would look like. I'll focus on the developer's side. I'll write more about how the browser implementation works in a future article.

These examples follow the current proposal. The API is still being developed and may change.

The API

Before getting into the examples, here's the API at a glance:

// Request access to a model.
navigator.models.requestAccess(model);

// Generate text, stream a response, or create embeddings.
navigator.models.generate(model, input);
navigator.models.stream(model, input);
navigator.models.embed(model, input);

// Bind a model for repeated calls.
navigator.models.session(model);

// Read model details after access has been granted.
navigator.models.info(model);
navigator.models.list();

For a more extensive look at the input and output styles for the api view the reference.

Use cases

The three examples: summarizing a page, creating embeddings, and drafting image descriptions.

I'll reuse this small helper to check support and request access:

async function requestModel(model) {
  if (!("models" in navigator)) {
    throw new Error("This browser does not support Web Models.");
  }
  const access = await navigator.models.requestAccess(model);
    if (access.status !== "granted") {
      throw new Error("Model access was not granted.");
    }
  }
}

Summarize page content

Let's add a summary button to a page that already contains an <article> element.

<button id="summarize" type="button">Summarize this article</button>
<p id="summary" role="status"></p>

const summarizeButton = document.querySelector("#summarize");
const summaryOutput = document.querySelector("#summary");
const textModel = "<text-model-id>";

summarizeButton.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  summarizeButton.disabled = true;
  summaryOutput.textContent = "";
  try {
    await requestModel(textModel);
    const article = document.querySelector("article")?.innerText;
    if (!article?.trim()) throw new Error("No article text was found.");
    const result = await navigator.models.generate(textModel, {
      messages: [
        { role: "system", content: "Summarize the supplied article in three short sentences." },
        { role: "user", content: article }
      ],
      maxOutputTokens: 200
    });
    if (result.finishReason !== "stop") {
      throw new Error("The summary did not finish. Try a shorter input or a larger output limit.");
    }
    summaryOutput.textContent = result.data ?? "";
  } catch (error) {
    summaryOutput.textContent = error.message;
  } finally {
    summarizeButton.disabled = false;
  }
});

The app reads its own page and passes the text to the model. The answer is in result.data. finishReason tells us whether it finished or reached a limit.

Create embeddings

Embeddings let us compare text by meaning. A search for "when is the launch?" could find a note that says "the release moved to October."

Here's how to turn a few notes into vectors:

<button id="index-notes" type="button">Create note embeddings</button>
<p id="index-status" role="status"></p>

const indexButton = document.querySelector("#index-notes");
const indexStatus = document.querySelector("#index-status");
const embeddingModel = "<embedding-model-id>";
const notes = [
  { id: 1, text: "The release moved to October." },
  { id: 2, text: "The design review is on Tuesday." },
  { id: 3, text: "Support hours are 9 AM to 5 PM." }
];
let noteIndex;

indexButton.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  indexButton.disabled = true;
  indexStatus.textContent = "";
  try {
    await requestModel(embeddingModel);
    const result = await navigator.models.embed(
      embeddingModel,
      notes.map(note => note.text)
    );
    noteIndex = {
      model: result.model,
      entries: notes.map((note, i) => ({
        ...note,
        vector: result.vectors[i]
      }))
    };
    console.log(noteIndex);
    indexStatus.textContent = `Created embeddings for ${notes.length} notes.`;
  } catch (error) {
    indexStatus.textContent = error.message;
  } finally {
    indexButton.disabled = false;
  }
});

embed() gives us a vector for each note. I've kept the model ID with them because we'll need the same model for search queries.

Accessibility tools

Let's have the model write a first draft of alt text for an image. We'll put it in a text field so the author can edit it before publishing.

I'm asking for a structured response here, so the model needs to support image input and JSON Schema output.

<label for="image-file">Choose an image</label>
<input id="image-file" type="file" accept="image/*">

<label for="image-context">How will this image be used?</label>
<input id="image-context" type="text">
<button id="describe-image" type="button">Draft alt text</button>
<label for="alt-draft">Alt text - review before publishing</label>
<textarea id="alt-draft"></textarea>
<p id="image-status" role="status"></p>

const describeButton = document.querySelector("#describe-image");
const altDraft = document.querySelector("#alt-draft");
const imageStatus = document.querySelector("#image-status");
const visionModel = "<vision-model-id>";

describeButton.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  describeButton.disabled = true;
  altDraft.value = "";
  imageStatus.textContent = "";
  try {
    const image = document.querySelector("#image-file").files[0];
    const context = document.querySelector("#image-context").value;
    if (!image) throw new Error("Choose an image first.");
    if (!context.trim()) throw new Error("Describe how the image will be used.");
    await requestModel(visionModel);
    const result = await navigator.models.generate(visionModel, {
      messages: [{
        role: "user",
        content: [
          { type: "text", text: `Draft concise alt text for this image. Avoid guessing details. Page context: ${context}` },
          { type: "image", image }
        ]
      }],
      output: {
        schema: {
          type: "object",
          properties: { alt: { type: "string" } },
          required: ["alt"],
          additionalProperties: false
        }
      },
      maxOutputTokens: 120
    });
    if (result.finishReason !== "stop") {
      throw new Error("The description did not finish. Try again with a larger output limit.");
    }
    altDraft.value = result.data.alt;
    imageStatus.textContent = "Draft ready for review.";
  } catch (error) {
    imageStatus.textContent = error.message;
  } finally {
    describeButton.disabled = false;
  }
});

The image comes straight from the file picker. Asking for an object with an alt field gives us result.data.alt, with no JSON string to parse.

Other ideas

  • Rewrite selected text in simpler language.
  • Extract fields from a receipt into a structured object.
  • Receipt organizer.
  • Choose a UI component based on generated content.
  • Use tool calls to filter a list or update a form, with the app checking and running each call.
  • Transcribe audio clips.
  • Offline privacy focused text-to-sql data explorer.

Final Thoughts

With this API, I could add these features to a web app without managing model downloads and execution in every project. This is still very much a proposal, but one that I believe is badly needed. If you're interested in helping move this forward, start by reading the explainer and API reference and joining the WICG discussion.

Web Models API — Models belong in every browser.

A proposed browser API for web apps that need a particular open-weight model. People control access; the browser runs it. Join the Web Models API discussion.
